chapters.title: Book 1, Chapter 1 — Subject of the First Book
paragraphs: I want to ask whether, in the civil order, there can be any sure and legitimate rule for governing, if we take people as they are and laws as they could be. As I do, I will always try to join what right permits with what interest requires, so that justice and utility are never split apart.

I begin without arguing that my subject matters. People will ask whether I am a prince or a legislator, that I should write about politics. My answer is that I am neither, and that is exactly why I write about it. If I were a prince or a legislator, I would not spend my time saying what ought to be done. I would do it, or say nothing.

I was born a citizen of a free State and a member of the Sovereign. However little my voice may count in public affairs, the right to vote on them makes it my duty to study them. And whenever I think about governments, I am glad to find that my studies keep giving me new reasons to love the government of my own country.

Man is born free, and yet everywhere he is in chains. One man believes he is the master of others, yet he is more of a slave than they are. How did this change come about? I do not know. What can make it legitimate? I believe I can answer that question.

If I took into account only force and what follows from it, I would say: “As long as a people is compelled to obey, and does obey, it does well. As soon as it is able to shake off the yoke, and does so, it does better still. For it regains its liberty by the same right by which that liberty was taken away, so either it is justified in taking it back, or there was never any justification for those who took it.” But the social order is a sacred right, and it is the basis of all other rights. This right, however, does not come from nature, so it must be founded on conventions. Before I come to that, I have to prove what I have just asserted.

chapters.title: Book 1, Chapter 2 — The First Societies
paragraphs: The oldest of all societies, and the only natural one, is the family. Even so, children stay tied to their father only as long as they need him to survive. When that need ends, the natural bond dissolves. The children are freed from the obedience they owed their father, and the father is freed from the care he owed his children, and all of them return to independence on equal terms. If they stay together, they do so no longer by nature but by choice, and the family itself is held together only by convention.

This common liberty comes from the nature of man. His first law is to look after his own survival, and his first concerns are the ones he owes to himself. Once he reaches the age of reason, he alone judges the right means of keeping himself alive, and so he becomes his own master.

The family, then, may be seen as the first model of political societies. The ruler is like the father, the people like the children; and since all are born free and equal, they give away their liberty only when it is to their own advantage. The one difference is this. In the family, the father’s love for his children pays him back for the care he gives them. In the State, the pleasure of commanding takes the place of that love, which the chief cannot feel for the many peoples under him.

Grotius denies that all human power is set up for the benefit of the governed, and he cites slavery as an example. His usual way of reasoning is always to base right on fact.[1] A more logical method would be possible, but none could be better for tyrants.

So, according to Grotius, it is doubtful whether the human race belongs to a hundred men, or those hundred men belong to the human race. Throughout his book he seems to lean toward the first view, and so does Hobbes. On this account, humanity is split into herds of cattle, each with a ruler who guards it only in order to devour it.

A shepherd is by nature superior to his flock, so the shepherds of men, _i.e._ their rulers, are by nature superior to the peoples under them. This, according to Philo, was the reasoning of the Emperor Caligula, who concluded with equal soundness either that kings were gods or that men were beasts.
Caligula’s reasoning matches that of Hobbes and Grotius. Aristotle had said it before any of them: men are not at all equal by nature; some are born for slavery and others to rule.

Aristotle was right, but he took the effect for the cause. Nothing is more certain than that anyone born into slavery is born for slavery. In their chains slaves lose everything, even the wish to get free. They come to love their servitude, just as the comrades of Ulysses loved living as beasts.[2] So if some people are slaves by nature, it is because others were first made slaves against nature. Force made the first slaves, and their cowardice kept them slaves.

I have said nothing about King Adam, or Emperor Noah, the father of the three great monarchs who shared out the universe among them, like the children of Saturn, whom some scholars have taken them to be. I hope my moderation will earn me due thanks. After all, I am a direct descendant of one of these princes, perhaps of the eldest branch; for all I know, a check of the titles might prove me the legitimate king of the human race. Whatever the case, no one can doubt that Adam was sovereign of the world, as Robinson Crusoe was of his island, for as long as he was its only inhabitant. And this empire had one advantage: the monarch, secure on his throne, had no rebellions, wars or conspirators to fear.

chapters.title: Book 1, Chapter 3 — The Right of the Strongest
paragraphs: The strongest is never strong enough to stay master forever, unless he turns strength into right and obedience into duty. From this comes the right of the strongest, a phrase that seems to be meant ironically yet is actually laid down as a basic principle. But will no one ever explain it to us? Force is a physical power, and I do not see what moral effect it could have. Yielding to force is an act of necessity, not of will — at most, an act of prudence. In what sense could it be a duty?

Suppose for a moment that this so-called “right” exists. I maintain that the only result is a heap of inexplicable nonsense. If force creates right, the effect changes along with the cause: any force greater than the first takes over its right. Once people can disobey without being punished, disobedience is legitimate. And since the strongest is always in the right, the only thing that matters is to make oneself the strongest. But what sort of right disappears when force fails? If we have to obey because we are forced, there is no need to obey because we ought to. And if we are not forced to obey, we have no obligation to. Clearly, then, the word “right” adds nothing to force. Here it means nothing at all.

Obey the powers that be. If this means yield to force, it is good advice but unnecessary, since I can promise it will never be broken. I admit that all power comes from God, but so does all sickness. Does that mean we are forbidden to call a doctor? A brigand surprises me at the edge of a wood. Am I merely forced to hand over my purse, or, even if I could keep it back, am I bound in conscience to give it up? After all, the pistol he holds is also a power.
So let us grant that force does not create right, and that we owe obedience only to legitimate powers. If so, we are back at my original question.

chapters.title: Book 1, Chapter 4 — Slavery
paragraphs: Nobody has any natural authority over other people, and force creates no right. That leaves conventions as the only basis for legitimate authority among men.

Grotius asks: if an individual can give up his liberty and become some master’s slave, why could an entire people not do likewise and become a king’s subjects? The passage is full of ambiguous words that would need explaining, but let us look only at the word _alienate_. To alienate means to give or to sell. A man who becomes another’s slave does not give himself away. He sells himself, at the least in exchange for his subsistence. But what does a people sell itself for? A king does not supply his subjects with their subsistence. He draws his own from them, and, as Rabelais says, kings do not live on nothing. So do subjects hand over their persons on condition that the king takes their possessions too? I fail to see what they have left to keep.

It will be said that the despot guarantees his subjects civil peace. Granted. But what do they gain from it if the wars his ambition brings down on them, his insatiable greed and the harassment of his ministers hurt them more than their own quarrels would have? What do they gain if the very peace they enjoy is one of their miseries? There is peace in dungeons too, but does that make dungeons good places to live? The Greeks shut up in the Cyclops’ cave lived there quite peacefully while they waited their turn to be eaten.

Saying that a man gives himself away for nothing means saying something absurd and inconceivable. An act like that is void and illegitimate for the plain reason that the man who does it is not in his right mind. Saying the same of a whole people means supposing a people of madmen, and madness creates no right.

Even if each man could give himself away, he could not give away his children. They are born men and free. Their liberty belongs to them, and no one but them has the right to dispose of it. Before they reach the age of reason, their father may, in their name, set conditions for their survival and well-being, but he cannot give them away irrevocably and unconditionally. Such a gift goes against the purposes of nature and exceeds a father’s rights. So to make an arbitrary government legitimate, the people in every generation would have to be free to accept or reject it. But if that were so, the government would no longer be arbitrary.

To renounce liberty is to renounce being a man, to give up the rights of humanity and even its duties. No compensation is possible for someone who gives up everything. Such a renunciation cannot be reconciled with man’s nature: to take all liberty from his will is to take all morality from his acts. Finally, a convention that sets up absolute authority on one side and unlimited obedience on the other is empty and self-contradictory. Is it not clear that we can have no obligation to a person from whom we have the right to demand everything? Does this condition alone, with no equivalence or exchange, not make the act void? For what right can my slave have against me, when everything he has belongs to me? His right being mine, a right of mine against myself is a phrase with no meaning.

Grotius and the others find another origin for the so-called right of slavery in war. They hold that the victor has the right to kill the vanquished, so the vanquished can buy back his life at the price of his liberty, and this convention is all the more legitimate because it benefits both parties.

But it is clear that nothing in the state of war supports this supposed right to kill the conquered. People who live in their original independence have no relations with one another stable enough to make up a state of peace or a state of war, so they cannot be natural enemies. War arises from a relation between things, not between persons. And a state of war cannot grow out of simple personal relations, only out of real relations. So private war, or war of man against man, cannot exist in the state of nature, where there is no settled property, or in the social state, where everything is under the authority of the laws.

Individual combats, duels and encounters are acts that cannot constitute a state. As for the private wars that the Establishments of Louis IX, King of France, authorized and the Peace of God suspended, they are abuses of feudalism, which is in itself as absurd a system as ever existed, and contrary to the principles of natural right and to all sound political order.

War, then, is not a relation between one man and another but between one State and another. Individuals are enemies only by accident: not as men, nor even as citizens,[1] but as soldiers; not as members of their country but as its defenders. Finally, each State can have only other States as enemies, not men, since there can be no real relation between things of different natures.

This principle also agrees with the established rules of every age and the constant practice of all civilized peoples. A declaration of war is a notice given less to the powers than to their subjects. A foreigner, whether king, individual or people, who robs, kills or detains subjects without having declared war on the prince is not an enemy but a brigand. Even in real war, a just prince seizes everything in the enemy’s country that belongs to the public, but respects the lives and goods of individuals; he respects the rights on which his own are founded. The aim of the war is to destroy the hostile State, so the other side has the right to kill its defenders for as long as they bear arms. But as soon as they lay them down and surrender, they cease to be enemies or instruments of the enemy and become simply men again, and no one has any right to take their lives. Sometimes it is possible to kill the State without killing a single one of its members; and war gives no right that is not necessary to achieving its aim. These principles are not those of Grotius. They do not rest on the authority of poets; they are derived from the nature of reality and founded on reason.

The right of conquest rests on nothing but the right of the strongest. War does not give the conqueror the right to massacre a conquered people. So he cannot ground a right to enslave them on a right that does not exist. A man may kill an enemy only when he cannot make him a slave, which means the right to enslave cannot come from the right to kill. It is therefore an unfair bargain to make the conquered buy back his life, which the victor has no right to take, by giving up his liberty. Is there not plainly a vicious circle in resting the right of life and death on the right of slavery, and the right of slavery on the right of life and death?

Even if we grant this terrible right to kill everybody, I maintain that a slave made in war, or a conquered people, owes its master nothing except obedience, and only as far as it is forced to obey. By accepting an equivalent for his life, the victor has done him no favor: instead of killing him pointlessly, he has killed him usefully. So far is he from gaining any authority over him beyond that of force that the state of war continues between them. Their relation is itself the effect of it, and exercising the right of war does not imply a treaty of peace. A convention has indeed been made, but far from ending the state of war, it presupposes that it continues.

So whichever way we look at the question, the right of slavery is null and void. It is not only illegitimate; it is absurd and means nothing. The words _slave_ and _right_ contradict each other and rule each other out. It will always be just as foolish for a man to say to another man, or to a whole people: “I make a convention with you that is entirely at your expense and entirely to my advantage. I will keep it as long as I please, and you will keep it as long as I please.”

chapters.title: Book 1, Chapter 5 — That We Must Always Go Back to a First Convention
paragraphs: Even if I conceded everything I have been arguing against, the friends of despotism would be no better off. Subduing a multitude is always very different from governing a society. Say that one man enslaves scattered individuals one after another, however many there are: I still see only a master and his slaves. I do not see a people and its ruler. What I see is a mere aggregate, not an association, with no public good and no body politic yet. That man may have enslaved half the world, but he is still a single individual, and his interest, apart from everyone else’s, is still purely private. When he dies, his empire is left as scattered and disunited as before, the way an oak collapses into a pile of ashes once fire has burned through it.

Grotius says that a people can give itself to a king. By that reasoning, a people is already a people before it gives itself away. The giving is itself a civil act, and it takes public deliberation. So before we examine how a people gives itself to a king, we should examine how it became a people in the first place. That earlier act must come first, and it is the true foundation of society.

Indeed, if there were no earlier convention, where would the minority’s obligation to accept the majority’s choice come from, unless the election were unanimous? What right have a hundred men who want a master to vote on behalf of ten who do not? The rule of majority voting is itself established by convention, and it presupposes unanimity on at least one occasion.

chapters.title: Book 1, Chapter 6 — The Social Compact
paragraphs: I suppose that men have reached the point where the obstacles to their survival in the state of nature prove stronger than the resources each individual has for staying alive in that state. That original condition can then no longer continue, and the human race would perish unless it changed its way of living.

But men cannot create new forces; they can only combine and direct the ones that exist. So the only way they have to preserve themselves is to form, by joining together, a sum of forces large enough to overcome the resistance. They must set these forces in motion through a single driving power and make them act in concert.

This sum of forces can arise only when several persons come together. But the force and liberty of each man are the chief instruments of his self-preservation. How can he commit them to the group without harming his own interests and neglecting the care he owes to himself? In terms of my present subject, this difficulty can be stated as follows —

“The problem is to find a form of association that protects and defends the person and property of each member with the full common force, and in which each person, though united with all the others, obeys only himself and stays as free as before.” This is the basic problem that the _Social Contract_ solves.

The terms of this contract are fixed so firmly by the nature of the act that the smallest change would make them void and useless. So even if they have perhaps never been formally declared, they are the same everywhere, and everywhere they are silently understood and accepted. They stay in force until the social compact is violated. Then each person recovers his original rights and goes back to his natural liberty, and he loses the conventional liberty he gave it up for.

Properly understood, these clauses can be reduced to one: the total transfer of each associate, with all his rights, to the whole community. For, in the first place, since each gives himself completely, the conditions are the same for everyone; and since they are the same for everyone, no one has any interest in making them burdensome to others.

Moreover, because the transfer is made without reserve, the union is as perfect as it can be, and no associate has anything further to claim. For if individuals kept certain rights, there would be no common superior to judge between them and the public. Each, being his own judge on one point, would soon ask to be his own judge on all. The state of nature would continue, and the association would inevitably become either ineffective or tyrannical.

Last, when each man gives himself to everyone, he gives himself to no one. And since he gains over every associate exactly the same right that he grants that associate over himself, he gets back the equivalent of all he loses, plus extra force to protect what he has.
If, then, we set aside everything in the social compact that is not essential to it, we shall find that it comes down to these terms —
_“Each of us places his person and all his power in common under the supreme direction of the general will, and we receive each member, as one body, as an indivisible part of the whole.”_

At once, this act of association replaces the individual person of each party to the contract with a moral and collective body. That body has as many members as the assembly has votes, and from the act it receives its unity, its shared identity, its life and its will. This public person, formed by the union of all the others, used to be called a _city_,[1] and is now called a _Republic_ or _body politic_. Its members call it the _State_ when it is passive, the _Sovereign_ when it is active, and a _Power_ when they compare it with others like itself. Those who are associated in it are collectively called the _people_. Individually they are called _citizens_ insofar as they share in the sovereign power, and _subjects_ insofar as they are under the laws of the State. These terms are often confused and used for one another, but it is enough to know how to tell them apart when precision matters.

This same mistake once cost the Carthaginians dearly. I have never read of the title of citizens being given to the subjects of any prince, not even to the ancient Macedonians or the English of today, although they are closer to liberty than anyone else. When Bodin wrote of our citizens and townsmen, he made a bad blunder by taking one class for the other. M. d’Alembert avoided that error. In his article on Geneva he clearly distinguished the four orders of men (or even five, counting mere foreigners) who live in our town, of which only two make up the Republic. No other French writer, to my knowledge, has understood the real meaning of the word citizen.

chapters.title: Book 1, Chapter 7 — The Sovereign
paragraphs: This formula shows that the act of association is a mutual commitment between the public and the individuals. Each individual is, so to speak, making a contract with himself, and so he is bound in two capacities: as a member of the Sovereign he is bound to individuals, and as a member of the State he is bound to the Sovereign. But the maxim of civil right that no one is bound by promises made to himself does not apply here. Owing an obligation to yourself is very different from owing one to a whole of which you are a part.

We must also point out that public deliberation can bind all the subjects to the Sovereign, because each of them can be seen in two different capacities. For the opposite reason, it cannot bind the Sovereign to itself. So it goes against the nature of the body politic for the Sovereign to impose on itself a law that it cannot break. The Sovereign can see itself in only one capacity, which puts it in the position of an individual making a contract with himself. That shows there neither is nor can be any kind of fundamental law binding the body of the people — not even the social compact itself. This does not mean the body politic cannot make commitments to others, as long as they do not violate the contract; for in relation to anything outside it, it becomes a single being, an individual.

But the body politic, or the Sovereign, draws its being wholly from the sanctity of the contract. So it can never bind itself, even to an outsider, to do anything that detracts from the original act, such as giving away some part of itself or submitting to another Sovereign. To violate the act by which it exists would be to destroy itself, and what is itself nothing can create nothing.

Once this multitude is united in one body, no one can wrong a single member without attacking the body, and still less can anyone wrong the body without its members feeling it. Duty and interest therefore bind both contracting parties equally to help each other, and the same men should seek to gather into their double capacity all the advantages that go with it.

Again, the Sovereign is made up entirely of the individuals who compose it. It has no interest contrary to theirs, and it cannot have one. So the sovereign power has no need to give its subjects any guarantee, because it is impossible for the body to want to hurt all its members. We shall also see later that it cannot hurt any one of them in particular. By its very nature, the Sovereign is always what it should be.

This is not the case, however, with the relation of the subjects to the Sovereign. Despite the common interest, the Sovereign would have no security that the subjects would fulfill their undertakings unless it found a means of making sure of their loyalty.

In fact, each individual, as a man, may have a particular will that is contrary or unlike the general will he holds as a citizen. His particular interest may speak to him very differently from the common interest. His absolute and naturally independent existence may lead him to see what he owes the common cause as a free gift, whose loss will hurt others less than paying it burdens him. And since the moral person that makes up the State is not a man, he may treat it as a persona ficta, and want to enjoy the rights of a citizen without being willing to carry out the duties of a subject. If such an injustice went on, it would inevitably ruin the body politic.

For the social compact not to be an empty formula, it silently includes one commitment, which alone can give force to the rest: anyone who refuses to obey the general will must be compelled to do so by the whole body. This means nothing less than that he will be forced to be free. That is the condition which, by giving each citizen to his country, shields him from all personal dependence. Here lies the key to how the political machine works. It alone makes civil commitments legitimate; without it they would be absurd, tyrannical and open to the most terrible abuses.

chapters.title: Book 1, Chapter 8 — The Civil State
paragraphs: The move from the state of nature to the civil state changes man in a remarkable way. Justice replaces instinct in his conduct, and his actions take on the morality they lacked before. Only then, when the voice of duty replaces physical impulse and right replaces appetite, does _man_, who until now had thought only of himself, find that he must act on different principles and consult his reason before following his inclinations. In this state he gives up some of the advantages nature gave him, but he gains far greater ones. His faculties are exercised and developed, his ideas broadened, his feelings elevated, and his whole soul lifted so high that, if the abuses of this new condition did not so often drag him below the one he left, he would have to bless forever the happy moment that pulled him out of it, and that turned him from a stupid, unimaginative animal into an intelligent being and a man.

Let us add up the whole account in terms that are easy to compare. By the social compact, man loses his natural liberty and his unlimited right to anything he tries to get and manages to get. He gains civil liberty and ownership of everything he possesses. To weigh one against the other without error, we must keep several distinctions clear. Natural liberty is bounded only by the strength of the individual, while civil liberty is limited by the general will. And possession is merely the result of force or of the right of the first occupier, while property can be founded only on a positive title.

Besides all this, we could add moral liberty to what man gains in the civil state. Moral liberty alone makes him truly his own master, since being driven by appetite alone is slavery, while obeying a law we prescribe for ourselves is liberty. But I have already said too much on this subject, and the philosophical meaning of the word liberty is not our concern here.

chapters.title: Book 1, Chapter 9 — Real Property
paragraphs: At the moment of its founding, each member gives himself to the community exactly as he is, with all the resources at his command, including the goods he owns. When possession changes hands in this act, it does not change its nature; it becomes property in the hands of the Sovereign. But the forces of the city are vastly greater than those of any individual, so public possession is also, in fact, stronger and more irrevocable, though no more legitimate, at least from the point of view of foreigners. Toward its members, the State is master of all their goods by the social compact, which within the State is the basis of every right. Toward other powers, however, it is master of them only by the right of the first occupier, which it holds from its members.

The right of the first occupier is more real than the right of the strongest, yet it becomes a true right only once the right of property has been established. By nature every man has a right to everything he needs. But the positive act that makes him owner of one thing shuts him out from everything else. His share is settled, so he should keep to it and has no further claim against the community. That is why the right of the first occupier, so weak in the state of nature, is respected by every man in civil society. What we respect in this right is less what belongs to another than what does not belong to us.

In general, three conditions are necessary to establish the right of the first occupier over a piece of land. First, the land must not yet be inhabited. Second, a man must occupy only as much as he needs to live on. Third, he must take possession not by an empty ceremony but by labor and cultivation, the only sign of ownership that others should respect in the absence of a legal title.

If we base the right of first occupancy on need and labor, are we not stretching it as far as it will go? Can such a right be left without limits? Is it enough to set foot on common ground in order to call yourself its master on the spot? Is it enough to have the strength to drive others off for a moment, in order to establish a right to keep them out forever? How can a man or a people seize a vast territory and keep it from the rest of the world, except by a punishable usurpation, when such an act robs everyone else of the home and the means of living that nature gave them all in common? When Nuñez Balboa stood on the seashore and took possession of the South Seas and all of South America in the name of the crown of Castile, was that enough to dispossess everyone who actually lived there and to shut out every prince in the world? If so, such ceremonies are repeated pointlessly, and the Catholic King need only take possession of the entire universe at once, from his own apartment, merely making a later reservation for whatever other princes already held.

We can picture how the lands of individuals, where they lay next to each other and came to be joined, became the public territory, and how the right of Sovereignty, reaching from the subjects out over the lands they held, became at once real and personal. This made the landholders more dependent, and the forces at their command became a guarantee of their loyalty. Ancient monarchs seem not to have noticed this advantage. They called themselves Kings of the Persians, Scythians or Macedonians, and seem to have thought of themselves more as rulers of men than as masters of a country. Those of today are cleverer: they call themselves Kings of France, Spain, England and so on. By holding the land, they feel quite sure of holding the inhabitants.

What is peculiar about this transfer is that, when the community takes over the goods of individuals, it does not strip them of anything; it only secures their legitimate possession, turning usurpation into true right and mere enjoyment into ownership. The possessors are then regarded as trustees of the public good. All the members of the State respect their rights, and all its forces defend those rights against foreign aggression. So by a cession that benefits the public, and benefits themselves even more, they have, so to speak, acquired everything they gave up. This paradox is easily explained by the distinction between the rights that the Sovereign and the owner have over the same estate, as we shall see later. It can also happen that men begin to unite with one another before they possess anything, and that they then occupy a stretch of country big enough for all, and either enjoy it in common or divide it among themselves, equally or in proportions set by the Sovereign. However the acquisition happens, each individual’s right to his own estate is always subordinate to the community’s right over everything. Without that, the social bond would have no stability, and the exercise of Sovereignty no real force.

I shall end this chapter and this book with a remark on which the whole social system should rest, _i.e._ that, instead of destroying natural inequality, the fundamental compact replaces whatever physical inequality nature may have set up between men with a moral and legitimate equality. Men who may be unequal in strength or intelligence all become equal by convention and legal right.[1]

chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 1 — That Sovereignty Is Inalienable
paragraphs: The first and most important consequence of the principles established so far is this: only the general will can direct the State toward the purpose for which it was founded, _i.e._ the common good. If the clash of particular interests made it necessary to form societies, the agreement of those same interests made it possible. What these different interests have in common is what forms the social tie, and if there were no point on which they all agreed, no society could exist. It is on this common interest alone that every society ought to be governed.

I hold, then, that Sovereignty is nothing other than the exercise of the general will, and so it can never be given away. The Sovereign is nothing other than a collective being, and so it can be represented only by itself. Power may be transferred, but not will.

In fact, it is not impossible for a particular will to agree with the general will on some point, but it is impossible for that agreement to be lasting and constant. The particular will tends by its nature toward partiality, while the general will tends toward equality. It is even more impossible to have any guarantee of such agreement. Even if it always existed, it would be the result of chance, not of design. The Sovereign may well say, “At this moment I will what this man wills, or at least what he says he wills.” But it cannot say, “What he wills tomorrow, I will too.” For it is absurd for the will to bind itself for the future, and no will is obliged to consent to anything that is against the good of the being who wills. If the people, then, simply promises to obey, it dissolves itself by that very act and loses what makes it a people. The moment there is a master, there is no longer a Sovereign, and from that moment the body politic has ceased to exist.

None of this rules out that the commands of the rulers may pass for the general will, provided the Sovereign is free to object and does not. In that case, the silence of everyone is taken as the consent of the people. I will explain this later.

chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 2 — That Sovereignty Is Indivisible
paragraphs: Sovereignty is indivisible for the same reason that it is inalienable. A will is either general or it is not,[1] and it is either the will of the whole body of the people or only of a part of it. In the first case, the declared will is an act of Sovereignty and makes law. In the second, it is only a particular will, or an act of magistracy — at most a decree.

But our political theorists cannot divide Sovereignty in principle, so they divide it by its object: into force and will, into legislative power and executive power, into rights of taxation, justice and war, into internal administration and the power to make foreign treaties. Sometimes they run all these parts together, and sometimes they separate them. They turn the Sovereign into a fantastic creature assembled from several pieces, as if they were building a man out of several bodies, one with eyes, one with arms, another with feet, and nothing else on any of them. We are told that the jugglers of Japan cut up a child in front of the spectators, throw the pieces into the air one after another, and the child comes down alive and whole. Our political theorists perform much the same trick. First they dismember the body politic with a sleight of hand worthy of a fair, and then they put it back together, we do not know how.

This error comes from lacking an exact notion of Sovereign authority, and from mistaking for parts of it what are only its emanations. For example, declaring war and making peace have been regarded as acts of Sovereignty. They are not, because neither act makes law. Each is only the application of a law, a particular act that decides how the law applies, as we shall see clearly once the idea attached to the word _law_ has been defined.

If we examined the other divisions the same way, we would find that whenever Sovereignty seems to be divided, we are being fooled. The rights taken to be parts of Sovereignty are all really subordinate to it, and they always presuppose supreme wills that they merely carry into effect.

No one can estimate how much confusion this lack of exactness has cast over the judgments of writers on political right, when they use their own principles to rule on the respective rights of kings and peoples. Anyone can see, in Chapters III and IV of the first book of Grotius, how that learned man and his translator Barbeyrac tangle themselves up in their own sophistries. They are afraid of saying too much or too little of what they think, and so of offending the interests they have to keep happy. Grotius was a refugee in France, unhappy with his own country, and eager to court Louis XIII, to whom his book is dedicated. He spares no effort to strip the peoples of all their rights and to hand them to kings by every artifice he can think of. This would also have suited Barbeyrac, who dedicated his translation to George I of England. Unfortunately, the expulsion of James II, which he called an “abdication,” forced him to be extremely guarded, to shuffle and to equivocate, so as not to make William a usurper. If these two writers had adopted the true principles, every difficulty would have disappeared and they would always have been consistent. But it would have been a sad truth to tell, and it would have won favor for them with no one except the people. Besides, truth is no road to fortune, and the people hands out no ambassadorships, no professorships and no pensions.

chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 3 — Whether the General Will Is Fallible
paragraphs: It follows from what came before that the general will is always right and aims at the public advantage. It does not follow that the people’s deliberations are always equally correct. We always want our own good, but we do not always see what it is. The people is never corrupted, but it is often deceived, and only then does it seem to will something bad.

There is often a big difference between the will of all and the general will. The general will looks only to the common interest. The will of all looks to private interest and is merely a sum of particular wills. But remove from these same wills the pluses and minuses that cancel each other out,[1] and what is left as the sum of the differences is the general will.

Suppose the people deliberate with adequate information and the citizens have no communication with one another. Then the grand total of their small differences always yields the general will, and the decision is always good. But when factions arise and partial associations form at the expense of the great association, the will of each association becomes general for its members and stays particular for the State. We can then say that there are no longer as many votes as there are men, only as many as there are associations. The differences are fewer and the result is less general. Finally, when one of these associations grows so large that it outweighs all the others, the result is no longer a sum of small differences but a single difference. Then there is no general will at all, and the opinion that prevails is purely particular.

Therefore, if the general will is to express itself, there must be no partial society within the State, and each citizen must think only his own thoughts.[2] That was indeed the sublime and unique system of the great Lycurgus. If partial societies do exist, the best course is to have as many as possible and to keep them from being unequal, as Solon, Numa and Servius did. Only these precautions can guarantee that the general will stays enlightened and that the people never deceives itself.

chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 4 — The Limits of the Sovereign Power
paragraphs: If the State is a moral person whose life lies in the union of its members, and if its most important concern is its own preservation, it needs a universal, compelling force to move and arrange each part in whatever way is best for the whole. Nature gives each man absolute power over all his limbs. In the same way, the social compact gives the body politic absolute power over all its members. This power, directed by the general will, is what bears the name of Sovereignty, as I have said.

But besides the public person, we have to consider the private persons who make it up, whose life and liberty are by nature independent of it. We must therefore distinguish clearly between the rights of the citizens and those of the Sovereign,[1] and between the duties citizens owe as subjects and the natural rights they should enjoy as men.

I admit that by the social compact each man gives away only that part of his powers, goods and liberty that it matters for the community to control. But it must also be granted that the Sovereign is the sole judge of what matters.

A citizen ought to perform every service he can for the State as soon as the Sovereign demands it. But the Sovereign, for its part, cannot impose on its subjects any fetters that are useless to the community, and cannot even wish to do so. For nothing can happen without a cause, whether by the law of reason or by the law of nature.

The commitments that bind us to the social body are binding only because they are mutual. Their nature is such that in fulfilling them we cannot work for others without also working for ourselves. Why is the general will always right, and why do all constantly will the happiness of each person? Only because everyone thinks of “each” as meaning himself, and thinks of himself when he votes for all. This proves that equality of rights, and the idea of justice that such equality produces, come from the preference each man gives to himself, and so from the very nature of man. It proves that the general will, to be truly general, must be general in its object as well as in its essence: it must come from all and apply to all. And it proves that the general will loses its natural rectitude when it is directed at some particular, determinate object, because then we are judging something foreign to us and have no true principle of equity to guide us.

Indeed, as soon as a question of particular fact or right comes up on a point that no general convention has settled, the matter becomes contentious. The individuals concerned are one party and the public is the other, yet I can see neither the law to follow nor the judge to decide. It would be absurd in such a case to propose referring the question to an express decision of the general will. That decision could only be the conclusion of one of the parties, and so, for the other party, it would be merely an external, particular will, inclined on this occasion to injustice and liable to error. Thus, just as a particular will cannot stand for the general will, the general will changes its own nature when its object is particular, and as a general will it cannot pass judgment on a man or a fact. Take the people of Athens, for instance, when they appointed or removed their rulers, voted honors to one man and penalties on another, and by a multitude of particular decrees carried out all the functions of government without distinction. In those cases the people no longer had a general will in the strict sense. They were acting no longer as Sovereign but as magistrate. This will seem to contradict current views, but I must be given time to set out my own.

From all this it should be clear that what makes a will general is less the number of voters than the common interest that unites them. Under this system each person necessarily submits to the conditions he imposes on others. This admirable agreement of interest and justice gives the common deliberations an equitable character. That character vanishes at once when a particular question is discussed, because there is no common interest to unite the judge’s ruling with the party’s and make them one.

Whichever way we approach our principle, we reach the same conclusion: the social compact sets up such an equality among the citizens that they all pledge themselves on the same conditions and so should all enjoy the same rights. Therefore, by the very nature of the compact, every “act of Sovereignty,” _i.e._ every authentic act of the general will, binds or favors all the citizens equally. The Sovereign recognizes only the body of the nation and makes no distinctions among those who compose it. What, then, strictly speaking, is an act of Sovereignty? It is not an agreement between a superior and an inferior, but an agreement between the body and each of its members. It is legitimate because it rests on the social compact, equitable because it is common to all, useful because it can have no object other than the general good, and stable because it is guaranteed by the public force and the supreme power. As long as subjects submit only to agreements of this kind, they obey no one but their own will. To ask how far the respective rights of the Sovereign and the citizens extend is to ask how far citizens can make commitments to themselves, each with all and all with each.

From this we can see that the sovereign power, absolute, sacred and inviolable as it is, does not and cannot go beyond the limits of the general conventions, and that every man may do as he pleases with whatever goods and liberty these conventions leave him. So the Sovereign never has the right to lay more burdens on one subject than on another, because then the matter becomes particular and falls outside its competence.

Once these distinctions are admitted, it is plainly untrue that individuals make any real renunciation in the social compact. On the contrary, the position they find themselves in as a result of the compact is better than the one they were in before. Instead of a renunciation they have made an advantageous exchange. In place of an uncertain, precarious way of living they have a better and more secure one. In place of natural independence they have liberty; in place of the power to harm others, security for themselves; and in place of their own strength, which others might overcome, a right that social union makes invincible. Their very life, which they have devoted to the State, is constantly protected by it. And when they risk their lives in the State’s defense, what are they doing but giving back what they received from it? What are they doing that they would not do more often, and with greater danger, in the state of nature, where they would inevitably have to fight battles, at risk of their lives, to defend the very means of their survival? All must fight for their country when it needs them, it is true, but then no one ever has to fight for himself. Do we not gain by taking on, for the sake of what gives us security, only some of the risks we would have to run for ourselves as soon as we lost it?

chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 5 — The Right of Life and Death
paragraphs: People often ask how individuals who have no right to dispose of their own lives can transfer to the Sovereign a right they do not possess. I think the difficulty in answering lies in the way the question is put. Every man has a right to risk his own life in order to preserve it. Has anyone ever said that a man who throws himself out of a window to escape a fire is guilty of suicide? Has that crime ever been charged to a man who dies in a storm, though he knew of the danger when he went on board?

The aim of the social compact is to preserve the people who enter into it. Whoever wills the end also wills the means, and the means involve some risks and even some losses. A man who wants to preserve his life at the expense of others should also be ready, when necessary, to give it up for their sake. Moreover, the law may ask the citizen to face a danger, and he is no longer the judge of it. When the prince says to him, “It is expedient for the State that you should die,” he ought to die. Only on that condition has he lived in security until now, and his life is no longer merely a bounty of nature but a gift the State has made conditionally.

The death penalty for criminals can be seen in much the same light. We consent to die if we ourselves become assassins, so that we will not fall victim to an assassin. In making this compact we are far from disposing of our own lives. We think only of securing them, and no one is to be assumed to expect, at that moment, to be hanged.

Again, every wrongdoer who attacks social rights becomes, through his crimes, a rebel and a traitor to his country. By violating its laws he ceases to be a member of it, and he even makes war on it. Then the State cannot survive alongside him, and one or the other must perish. When we put the guilty man to death, we kill an enemy more than a citizen. The trial and judgment prove that he has broken the social compact, and so he is no longer a member of the State. He acknowledged himself a member by living there, so he must be removed from it: by exile, as a violator of the compact, or by death, as a public enemy. For such an enemy is not a moral person but merely a man, and in such a case the right of war is to kill the vanquished.

But, someone will say, condemning a criminal is a particular act. I grant it. Yet condemnation is not a function of the Sovereign. The Sovereign can confer that right without being able to exercise it itself. All my ideas fit together, but I cannot set them all out at once.

We may add that frequent punishments always signal weakness or laxity on the part of the government. There is no wrongdoer who could not be made good for something. The State has no right to put anyone to death, even to set an example, if it can leave him alive without danger.

Only the authority above both judge and law, _i.e._ the Sovereign, has the right to pardon, that is, to release the guilty from a penalty the law has set and the judge has pronounced. Even this right is far from clear, and the occasions for using it are extremely rare. In a well-governed State there are few punishments, not because there are many pardons but because criminals are rare. When a State is in decay, the sheer number of crimes guarantees impunity. Under the Roman Republic, neither the Senate nor the Consuls ever tried to pardon, and even the people never did, though it sometimes reversed its own decision. Frequent pardons mean that crime will soon have no need of them, and no one can fail to see where that leads. But I feel my heart protesting and holding back my pen. Let us leave these questions to the just man who has never offended and would himself never need pardon.

chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 6 — Law
paragraphs: The social compact gave the body politic existence and life. Legislation must now give it movement and will, because the original act that formed and united the body does not settle at all what the body should do to preserve itself.

What is good and orderly is so by the nature of things, whatever human agreements say. All justice comes from God, its only source. If we knew how to receive such a high inspiration, we would need no government and no laws. There is, no doubt, a universal justice that springs from reason alone. But for us to accept it, it has to work both ways. Speaking in human terms, the laws of justice have no force among men when nature supplies no sanctions: they only help the wicked and hurt the just, if the just man obeys them toward everyone while nobody obeys them toward him. So conventions and laws are needed to tie rights to duties and to bring justice to its proper object. In the state of nature, where everything is common, I owe nothing to anyone I have promised nothing; I recognize as belonging to others only what is of no use to me. In the state of society the law fixes all rights, and things are different.

But what, after all, is a law? So long as we only attach purely metaphysical ideas to the word, we will keep arguing without understanding one another. And even once we have defined a law of nature, we will be no closer to defining a law of the State.

I have already said that no general will can be directed at a particular object. That object must lie either inside the State or outside it. If it lies outside, a will that is foreign to the State is not general with respect to it. If it lies inside, it is part of the State, and then a relation arises between whole and part that makes them two separate beings: the part is one, and the whole minus that part is the other. But the whole minus a part is not the whole. As long as this relation lasts there is no whole, only two unequal parts, and so the will of one is no longer in any respect general toward the other.

But when the whole people makes decrees for the whole people, it considers only itself. If any relation arises, it is between two aspects of one entire object, and the whole is not divided. Then the subject of the decree is general, just as the will that decrees it is general. This act is what I call a law.

When I say that the object of laws is always general, I mean that a law looks at subjects _en masse_ and at actions in the abstract, never at a particular person or a particular action. So a law can decree that there will be privileges, but it cannot grant them to anyone by name. It can create several classes of citizens and even set the qualifications for each class, but it cannot say which persons belong to them. It can establish a monarchical government with hereditary succession, but it cannot pick a king or name a royal family. In short, any function that has a particular object lies outside the legislative power.

From this view it follows at once that nobody needs to ask whose business it is to make laws, since they are acts of the general will; or whether the prince is above the law, since he is a member of the State; or whether the law can be unjust, since no one is unjust to himself; or how we can be free and yet subject to the laws, since they only record our own wills.

We see further that the law joins a universal will to a universal object. So whatever a man, whoever he is, commands on his own account cannot be a law. Even what the Sovereign commands about a particular matter comes no closer to being a law: it is a decree, an act not of sovereignty but of magistracy.

I therefore call every State that is governed by laws a ‘Republic,’ whatever its form of administration may be. Only there does the public interest govern and the _res publica_ count as a _reality_. Every legitimate government is republican;[1] I will explain later what government is.

Laws are, strictly speaking, nothing but the conditions of civil association. The people who are subject to the laws ought to be their authors, and only those who join together to form the society should set its conditions. But how are they to set them? By common agreement, on a sudden inspiration? Does the body politic have an organ to declare its will? Who will give it the foresight to draft its acts and announce them in advance? Or how will it announce them when the need arises? How can a blind multitude, which often does not know what it wants because it rarely knows what is good for it, carry out by itself an undertaking as great and difficult as a system of legislation? On its own, the people always wills the good, but on its own it does not always see it. The general will is always right, but the judgment that guides it is not always enlightened. The people must be made to see things as they are, and sometimes as they ought to appear to it. It must be shown the good road it is searching for, shielded from the seductions of individual wills, taught to see times and places as a series, and made to weigh the pull of present, visible advantages against the danger of distant, hidden evils. Individuals see the good and reject it; the public wills the good and does not see it. Both need guidance. The first must be forced to bring their wills into line with their reason; the second must be taught to know what it wills. When that is done, public enlightenment unites understanding and will in the social body, so that the parts work together exactly and the whole is raised to its greatest strength. This is what makes a legislator necessary.

chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 7 — The Legislator
paragraphs: To find the rules of society that suit nations best, we would need a superior intelligence that could see all of men’s passions without feeling any of them. It would have to have no kinship with our nature, yet know it thoroughly. Its happiness would have to be independent of ours, and yet it would have to be willing to care about ours. And finally, it would have to look ahead to a distant glory as time goes by, working in one century and able to enjoy the result in another.[1] It would take gods to give men laws.

Caligula argued from the facts what Plato, in his dialogue the _Politicus_, argued from right when he defined the civil or kingly man. But if great princes are rare, great legislators are far rarer. A prince has only to follow the pattern a legislator must lay down. The legislator is the engineer who invents the machine; the prince is merely the mechanic who assembles it and keeps it running. “At the birth of societies,” says Montesquieu, “the leaders of Republics create the institutions, and afterward the institutions form the leaders.”[2]

Anyone who dares to set up the institutions of a people must feel able, so to speak, to change human nature. He must be able to turn each individual, who is by himself a complete and solitary whole, into a part of a larger whole from which that individual in some way receives his life and being. He must be able to alter man’s constitution in order to strengthen it, and to put a partial, moral existence in place of the physical and independent existence that nature gave us all. In a word, he must take away man’s own resources and give him new ones that are foreign to him and that he cannot use without the help of others. The more completely these natural resources are destroyed, the greater and more lasting are the ones he acquires, and the more solid and perfect the institutions. So when each citizen is nothing and can do nothing without all the others, and the resources acquired by the whole equal or exceed the sum of all the individuals’ resources, we may say that legislation has reached the highest point of perfection it can.

In every respect the legislator holds an extraordinary position in the State. He holds it through his genius, and just as much through his office, which is neither magistracy nor Sovereignty. This office, which establishes the Republic, has no place anywhere in its constitution. It is a singular, superior function with nothing in common with human rule. For if the one who commands men should not command the laws, then the one who commands the laws should not command men either. Otherwise his laws would be servants of his passions and would often only perpetuate his injustices, and his private aims would inevitably spoil the sanctity of his work.

When Lycurgus gave laws to his country, he began by giving up the throne. Most Greek towns customarily left the drafting of their laws to foreigners. The Republics of modern Italy often followed this example, and Geneva did too, to its benefit.[3] At the height of its prosperity, Rome saw every crime of tyranny come back to life and came close to destruction, because it put legislative authority and sovereign power in the same hands.

Yet the decemvirs themselves never claimed the right to pass any law on their own authority alone. “Nothing we propose to you,” they told the people, “can become law without your consent. Romans, make yourselves the authors of the laws that are to bring you happiness.”

So the person who drafts the laws has no right to legislate, or should have none. And the people cannot give up this right even if they want to, because it cannot be passed to anyone else: under the fundamental compact only the general will binds individuals, and there is no way to be sure that a particular will agrees with the general will until it has been put to the free vote of the people. I have said this before, but it is worth repeating.
So the work of legislation brings together two things that seem incompatible: an undertaking beyond human powers, and, to carry it out, an authority that is no authority.

There is a further difficulty worth noting. Wise men who try to address the common herd in their own language rather than the herd’s cannot possibly be understood. There are a thousand kinds of ideas that cannot be put into popular language. Ideas that are too general and objects that are too remote are equally out of its reach. Each individual cares only for the plan of government that serves his own interest, and finds it hard to see the benefits he might draw from the constant sacrifices that good laws demand. For a young people to appreciate sound principles of political theory and follow the basic rules of statecraft, the effect would have to become the cause. The social spirit, which the institutions are meant to create, would have to guide their very founding, and men would have to be, before the law, what the law is to make them. The legislator therefore cannot appeal to force or to reason, and must turn to an authority of a different kind, one that can compel without violence and persuade without convincing.

This is what has always driven the founders of nations to appeal to divine intervention and to credit the gods with their own wisdom. They did so in order that peoples, obeying the laws of the State as they obey the laws of nature, and recognizing the same power in the making of the city as in the making of man, might obey freely and bear the yoke of the public happiness submissively.

This sublime reason, far beyond the reach of the common herd, is the reason whose decisions the legislator puts in the mouths of the immortals, in order to compel by divine authority those whom human prudence could not move.[4] But not everyone can make the gods speak, or be believed when he declares himself their interpreter. The great soul of the legislator is the one miracle that can prove his mission. Any man can carve stone tablets, buy an oracle, claim secret communion with some god, train a bird to whisper in his ear, or find other crude ways to deceive the people. Someone whose knowledge goes no further may gather a band of fools, but he will never found an empire, and his extravagances will soon die with him. Idle tricks create only a passing bond; only wisdom can make one last. The Judaic law, which still survives, and the law of the child of Ishmael, which has ruled half the world for ten centuries, still proclaim the great men who laid them down. And while the pride of philosophy and the blind spirit of faction see in them nothing but lucky impostures, the true political theorist admires in the institutions they founded the great and powerful genius that presides over things built to last.

From this we should not conclude, as Warburton does, that politics and religion share a common object among us. The conclusion is rather that in the earliest periods of nations, one is used as an instrument of the other.

chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 8 — The People
paragraphs: Before building something large, an architect surveys the ground and tests it to see whether it can carry the weight. In the same way, the wise legislator does not begin by writing laws that are good in themselves. He begins by examining whether the people they are intended for can accept them. Plato refused to make laws for the Arcadians and the Cyrenaeans, because he knew both peoples were rich and could not tolerate equality. And good laws and bad men existed side by side in Crete, because Minos had imposed discipline on a people already burdened with vice.

A thousand nations have reached greatness on earth without ever being able to endure good laws. Even those that could have endured them could have done so only for a very short stretch of their long history. Most peoples, like most men, are docile only when young; as they grow old they become incorrigible. Once customs are fixed and prejudices deeply rooted, trying to reform them is dangerous and pointless. The people is like a foolish, cowardly patient who raves at the sight of the doctor, and can no longer bear to have anyone touch its faults in order to cure them.

Sometimes, indeed, in the history of States, violence and revolution do to whole peoples what certain illnesses do to individuals, turning their heads and making them forget the past. Horror of the past takes the place of forgetfulness, and the State, set on fire by civil wars, is born again, so to speak, from its ashes, and, fresh from the jaws of death, recovers the vigor of youth. Such were Sparta at the time of Lycurgus, Rome after the Tarquins, and, in modern times, Holland and Switzerland after the expulsion of the tyrants.

But such events are rare. They are exceptions, and the cause is always found in the particular constitution of the State concerned. They cannot even happen twice to the same people: a people can free itself while it is still barbarous, but not once the civic impulse has lost its force. Then disorder may destroy it, but revolutions cannot repair it. It needs a master, not a liberator. Free peoples, remember this maxim: “Liberty may be gained, but can never be recovered.”

Youth is not infancy. Nations, like men, have a period of youth, or, we might say, maturity, before which they should not be subjected to laws. But the maturity of a people is not always easy to recognize, and if it is anticipated, the work is spoiled. One people can be disciplined from the start; another cannot, even after ten centuries. Russia will never be truly civilized, because it was civilized too soon. Peter had a talent for imitation, but he lacked true genius, which is creative and makes everything out of nothing. Some of what he did was good, but most of it was out of place. He saw that his people were barbarous, but not that they were unripe for civilization. He wanted to civilize them when they needed only to be hardened. His first wish was to make Germans or Englishmen when he should have been making Russians, and by persuading his subjects that they were what they are not, he kept them from ever becoming what they might have been. A French tutor does the same: he turns his pupil into a child prodigy and then into nothing at all for the rest of his life. The empire of Russia will aspire to conquer Europe, and will itself be conquered. The Tartars, its subjects or neighbors, will become its masters and ours, through a revolution that I regard as inevitable. Indeed, all the kings of Europe are working together to hasten its coming.

chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 9 — The People (continued)
paragraphs: Nature sets limits to the stature of a well-formed man and, beyond those limits, produces only giants or dwarfs. In the same way, for a State to have the best possible constitution, one can fix limits that keep it from being too large to be well governed and too small to maintain itself. Every body politic has a _maximum_ strength that it cannot exceed and that it only loses by growing larger. The more the social tie is stretched, the looser it becomes; and in general a small State is stronger, in proportion to its size, than a large one.

Many arguments support this principle. First, distance makes administration harder, the way a weight gets heavier at the end of a longer lever. The greater the distance, the heavier the burden of administration. That is because each city has its own administration, which the people pay for; each district has its own, which the people also pay for; then come the provinces, and then the great governments, the satrapies and viceroyalties, which cost more the higher you go, always at the expense of the unfortunate people. Last of all comes the supreme administration, which overshadows all the rest. All these added costs are a constant drain on the subjects. Far from being better governed by all these different levels, they are worse governed than they would be under a single authority. Meanwhile hardly any resources remain for emergencies, and when the State has to draw on them, it is always on the verge of ruin.

There is more. A distant government has less vigor and speed in making sure the laws are obeyed, in preventing nuisances, correcting abuses and stopping rebellious plots that begin in faraway places. The people, for their part, feel less affection for rulers they never see, for a country that looks to them like the whole world, and for fellow citizens most of whom are strangers. The same laws cannot suit so many different provinces, with their different customs, their widely varied climates, and their inability to bear a uniform government. Different laws only breed trouble and confusion among peoples who share the same rulers, stay in constant contact, mix and intermarry, and, coming under new customs, never know whether even their own inheritance is really theirs. Talent is buried, virtue goes unknown and vice goes unpunished, among such a multitude of men who do not know one another, crowded together at the seat of the central administration. The leaders, swamped with business, see nothing for themselves, and the State is run by clerks. Finally, the measures needed to maintain the central authority, which all those distant officials either want to escape or want to exploit, use up all the energy of the public, so that none is left for the happiness of the people. There is barely enough to defend it when the need comes, and so a body too big for its constitution collapses, crushed under its own weight.

Again, the State must give itself a secure foundation if it is to be stable, to withstand the shocks it cannot help suffering, and to bear the efforts it will be forced to make to sustain itself. For all peoples have a kind of centrifugal force that makes them constantly act against one another and tend to grow at their neighbors’ expense, like the vortices of Descartes. The weak therefore risk being swallowed up soon, and it is almost impossible for any State to preserve itself except by putting itself in a kind of equilibrium with all the others, so that the pressure on it is practically equal on every side.

So there are reasons to expand and reasons to contract, and it takes no small skill in a statesman to find, between them, the middle course that best preserves the State. The reason for expansion is only external and relative, so it should rank below the reasons for contraction, which are internal and absolute. The first thing to look for is a strong and healthy constitution, and it is better to rely on the vigor that good government produces than on the resources of a large territory.

I should add that some States are known to have been constituted so that the need to make conquests was built into their very constitution, and that to survive they had to expand without end. Perhaps they congratulated themselves on this lucky necessity. Yet it showed them, together with the limit of their greatness, the unavoidable moment of their fall.

chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 10 — The People (continued)
paragraphs: A body politic can be measured in two ways: by the size of its territory or by the number of its people. There is a right relation between the two that makes a State truly great. Men make the State, and the land feeds the men. So the right relation is that the land should be enough to support its inhabitants, and that there should be as many inhabitants as the land can support. In this proportion a given number of people has its _maximum_ strength. If there is too much land, it is hard to guard and badly cultivated, it yields more than is needed, and it soon leads to defensive wars. If there is too little, the State depends on its neighbors for the surplus it lacks, and that soon leads to offensive wars. Any people whose situation leaves it a choice only between commerce and war is weak in itself. It depends on its neighbors and on circumstances, and its existence can never be more than short and uncertain. Either it conquers others and changes its situation, or it is conquered and becomes nothing. Only insignificance or greatness can keep it free.

No fixed relation can be stated between a territory and the population that suits it. Land differs in quality, fertility, products and climate, and the people who live on it differ in temperament: in a fertile country some consume little, while on poor soil others consume a great deal. One must also consider how fertile the women are, which conditions in each country help or hinder the growth of population, and how much the legislator can hope to influence it through his institutions. So the legislator should judge not by what he sees but by what he foresees, and should look not so much to the population he actually finds as to the one it ought naturally to reach. Finally, there are countless cases where particular local circumstances demand or permit a larger territory than seems necessary. A people will spread widely in mountain country, where the natural products, _i.e._ woods and pastures, need less labor, where experience shows that women are more fertile than on the plains, and where a great stretch of slope offers only a small level area that can be counted on to grow crops. On the coast, by contrast, a people can make do with less land, even among rocks and nearly barren sand, because fishing largely makes up for the lack of farm produce, because the inhabitants must live closer together to fight off pirates, and because it is easier to send the country’s surplus inhabitants abroad as colonies.

One more condition must be added to these requirements for giving laws. It cannot take the place of the others, but without it they are all useless: the enjoyment of peace and plenty. The moment when a State puts its house in order is like the moment when a battalion is forming up. Its body is then least able to resist and easiest to destroy. It would resist better in total disorganization than in a moment of ferment, when everyone is busy with his own position instead of the danger. If war, famine or sedition breaks out in this critical time, the State is certain to be overthrown.

Many governments have indeed been set up during such storms, but those governments themselves destroy the State. Usurpers always bring on or pick troubled times so that, under cover of public terror, they can pass destructive laws the people would never adopt in cold blood. The timing is one of the surest ways to tell a legislator’s work from a tyrant’s.

What people, then, is ready to receive laws? It is one already joined by some unity of origin, interest or convention, yet one that has never felt the true yoke of law. It has no deeply rooted customs or superstitions. It does not fear being overwhelmed by a sudden invasion. Without joining in its neighbors’ quarrels, it can resist each of them on its own, or win the help of one to drive off another. Every member can be known by every other, and no man needs to be given a burden too heavy for one man to carry. It can do without other peoples, and every other people can do without it;[1] it is neither rich nor poor but self-sufficient; and finally it combines the stability of an ancient people with the docility of a new one. What makes legislation hard is less what must be built than what must be torn down, and what makes success so rare is the impossibility of finding natural simplicity together with the needs of society. These conditions are rarely found all together, and so few States have good constitutions.

Europe still has one country capable of receiving laws: Corsica. The courage and persistence with which that brave people won back and defended its liberty deserve to have some wise man teach it how to keep what it has won. I have a feeling that one day that little island will astonish Europe.
