The Republic of Thlascala, surrounded by the Mexican Empire, preferred to go without salt rather than buy it from the Mexicans, or even take it from them as a gift. The Thlascalans were wise enough to see the trap hidden in such generosity. They kept their freedom, and that little State, shut up inside that great Empire, ended up as the instrument of its ruin.

chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 11 — The Various Systems of Legislation
paragraphs: If we ask what exactly the greatest good of all is, the good every system of legislation should aim at, we will find that it comes down to two main things: liberty and equality. Liberty, because every particular dependence removes that much force from the body of the State; and equality, because liberty cannot exist without it.

I have already defined civil liberty. By equality we should understand not that power and wealth must be exactly the same for everyone, but that power should never be great enough for violence and should always be exercised through rank and law; and that, as for wealth, no citizen should be rich enough to buy another, and none so poor that he is forced to sell himself:[1] which means that the great must show moderation in goods and position, and the common sort must show moderation in greed and covetousness.

People tell us that such equality is an impractical ideal that cannot really exist. But if it will inevitably be abused, does it follow that we should not at least regulate it? Precisely because circumstances tend constantly to destroy equality, legislation should always work to maintain it.

These general aims of every good legislative system must be adapted in each country to its local situation and to the temperament of its inhabitants. These circumstances should decide, in each case, which particular system of institutions is best, perhaps not in itself, but for the State it is meant for. If the soil is barren and unproductive, or the country too crowded for its inhabitants, the people should turn to industry and the crafts, and trade what they make for the goods they lack. If instead a people lives on rich plains and fertile slopes, or, in a good land, has too few inhabitants, it should give all its attention to agriculture, which makes people multiply, and should drive out the crafts, which would only depopulate the country by gathering the few inhabitants there are into a few places.[2] If a nation lives on a long and convenient coastline, let it cover the sea with ships and foster commerce and navigation. Its life will be short and glorious. If the sea on its coasts washes against nothing but almost inaccessible rocks, let it remain barbarous and live on fish. Its life will be quieter, perhaps better, and certainly happier. In a word, besides the principles all nations share, every nation has something in itself that determines how they apply and makes its legislation its own. So among the Jews long ago, and more recently among the Arabs, the chief object was religion; among the Athenians, letters; at Carthage and Tyre, commerce; at Rhodes, shipping; at Sparta, war; at Rome, virtue. The author of _The Spirit of the Laws_ has shown with many examples the art by which the legislator steers the constitution toward each of these objects.

What makes a State’s constitution truly solid and lasting is careful respect for what is fitting, so that natural relations and the laws always agree on every point, and law only serves, so to speak, to secure, accompany and correct those relations. But suppose the legislator mistakes his object and adopts a principle other than the one circumstances naturally point to. Suppose his principle makes for servitude where they make for liberty, or for wealth where they make for a large population, or for peace where they make for conquest. Then the laws will insensibly lose their influence, the constitution will change, and the State will have no rest from trouble until it is either destroyed or changed, and nature has resumed her invincible sway.

From the one come the friends of tyranny, and from the other, tyrants. It is always between them that public liberty is put up for auction: the one buys, and the other sells.

chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 12 — The Division of the Laws
paragraphs: To set the whole in order and give the commonwealth the best possible shape, we must consider several relations. The first is the action of the whole body on itself, the relation of the whole to the whole, of the Sovereign to the State. As we will see, this relation is made up of the relations of the intermediate terms.

The laws that govern this relation are called political laws, and also fundamental laws, with good reason if they are wise. If each State has only one good system, the people who have it should hold fast to it. But if the established order is bad, why should laws that keep men from being good count as fundamental? In any case, a people can always change its laws, however good they are. If a people chooses to harm itself, who has a right to stop it?

The second relation is that of the members to one another, or to the body as a whole. In the first respect the relation should be as slight as possible, and in the second as strong as possible. Each citizen would then be perfectly independent of all the others and, at the same time, very dependent on the city. The same means always brings this about, since only the strength of the State can secure its members’ liberty. Civil laws arise from this second relation.

We can also consider a third kind of relation, between the individual and the law: the relation of disobedience to its penalty. This leads to the creation of criminal laws, which are at bottom less a separate class of law than the sanction behind all the others.

Beside these three kinds of law stands a fourth, the most important of all. It is engraved not on tablets of marble or brass but on the hearts of the citizens. This is the State’s real constitution. It gains new strength every day. When other laws weaken or die out, it revives them or takes their place; it keeps a people on the path it was meant to follow, and insensibly replaces authority with the force of habit. I mean morals, custom, and above all public opinion, a power political thinkers do not know, yet on which success in everything else depends. The great legislator attends to this in secret, though he seems to limit himself to particular regulations. Those are only the curve of the arch, while manners and morals, slower to arise, finally form its immovable keystone.
Of the different classes of laws, only the political laws, which determine the form of the government, concern my subject.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 1 — Government in General
paragraphs: Before we discuss the different forms of government, let us pin down exactly what the word means. No one has yet explained it very clearly.
A warning to the reader: this chapter needs close reading. I cannot make myself clear to anyone who will not pay attention.

Every free action is produced by two causes working together. One is moral, _i.e._ the will that decides on the act; the other is physical, _i.e._ the power that carries it out. When I walk toward an object, I must first will to go there, and second, my feet must carry me. If a paralytic wills to run and an able-bodied man wills not to, both will stay where they are. The body politic has the same motive powers. Here too force and will are distinguished: will under the name of legislative power, and force under the name of executive power. Without both working together, nothing is done, or should be done.

We have seen that the legislative power belongs to the people and to no one else. The executive power, by contrast, cannot belong to the people as a whole acting as legislator or Sovereign, as the principles above make easy to see. It consists entirely of particular acts, and particular acts lie outside the reach of law, and so outside the reach of the Sovereign, whose acts must always be laws.

So the public force needs an agent of its own, one that gathers it together and sets it to work under the direction of the general will. This agent acts as a channel of communication between the State and the Sovereign, and does for the collective person roughly what the union of soul and body does for a human being. That is the basis of government in the State. People often confuse it, wrongly, with the Sovereign, though it is only the Sovereign’s minister.

What, then, is government? It is an intermediate body set up between the subjects and the Sovereign so that the two can correspond with each other. It is charged with carrying out the laws and maintaining liberty, both civil and political.

The members of this body are called magistrates or _kings_, that is to say _governors_, and the body as a whole is called the _prince_.[1] So those who say that a people’s act of putting itself under a prince is not a contract are quite right. It is only a commission, a job. The rulers are mere officials of the Sovereign, and they use in their own name a power that the Sovereign has made them trustees of. The Sovereign can limit this power, change it or take it back whenever it likes. Giving away such a right is incompatible with the nature of the social body and contrary to the purpose of association.
So I use the word _government_, or supreme administration, for the lawful exercise of the executive power. The man or body entrusted with that administration I call the prince or magistrate.

In government lie the intermediate forces whose relations make up the relation of the whole to the whole, that is, of the Sovereign to the State. We can picture this last relation as the two outer terms of a continuous proportion, with government as its mean proportional. Government takes from the Sovereign the orders it gives the people. For the State to be properly balanced, once everything is taken into account, the product or power of the government in itself must equal the product or power of the citizens, who are on the one hand sovereign and on the other subject.

Moreover, change any one of these three terms and the equality is destroyed at once. Suppose the Sovereign wants to govern, or the magistrate wants to make laws, or the subjects refuse to obey. Then order gives way to disorder, force and will stop acting together, and the State dissolves into despotism or anarchy. And since each relation has only one mean proportional, a State can have only one good government. But countless events can change a people’s relations. So different governments may be good for different peoples, and also for the same people at different times.
To give some idea of the various relations that can hold between these two extreme terms, I shall use the size of a people as my example, since it is the easiest to put into numbers.

Suppose the State has ten thousand citizens. The Sovereign can be considered only collectively, as a body. But each member, as a subject, counts as an individual. So the Sovereign stands to the subject as ten thousand to one, _i.e._ each member of the State has only a ten-thousandth share of the sovereign authority, though he is wholly under its control. If the people numbers a hundred thousand, the subject’s condition does not change. Each is still under the full authority of the laws, but his vote, now only one hundred-thousandth, has ten times less influence in drawing them up. The subject always remains a single unit, so his relation to the Sovereign grows with the number of citizens. It follows that the larger the State, the less the liberty.

By saying the relation increases, I mean that it becomes more unequal. So the larger it is in the geometrical sense, the smaller it is in the everyday sense of the word. In the geometrical sense, relation is judged by quantity and expressed by the quotient; in the everyday sense, it is judged by identity and measured by likeness.

Now, the less the particular wills have to do with the general will, that is, morals and manners with the laws, the more the repressive force must grow. So for government to be good, it must be proportionately stronger as the people becomes more numerous.

On the other hand, as the State grows, those who hold public authority face more temptations and get more chances to abuse their power. So the more force the government needs to keep the people in hand, the more force the Sovereign needs to keep the government in hand. I mean not absolute force but the relative force of the different parts of the State.

This double relation shows that the continuous proportion among the Sovereign, the prince and the people is not an arbitrary idea at all, but a necessary consequence of the nature of the body politic. It also follows that one of the extreme terms, the people as subject, is fixed and represented by unity. So whenever the duplicate ratio rises or falls, the simple ratio rises or falls with it, and changes accordingly. We can see from this that there is no single, absolute form of government. There are as many governments, differing in nature, as there are States differing in size.

Suppose someone, ridiculing this system, were to say that, according to me, finding the mean proportional and giving form to the body of government requires only finding the square root of the number of the people. I would answer that I am taking this number here only as an example; that the relations I am speaking of are measured not by the number of men alone but generally by the amount of action, which is a combination of a multitude of causes; and that, if I borrow the terms of geometry for a moment to save words, I am nonetheless well aware that moral quantities do not allow of geometrical accuracy.

The government is, on a small scale, what the body politic containing it is on a large one. It is a moral person with certain faculties, active like the Sovereign and passive like the State, and it can be resolved into other similar relations. This gives rise to a new proportion, and inside it yet another, according to how the magistracies are arranged, until we reach an indivisible middle term, _i.e._ a single ruler or supreme magistrate, who can be pictured in the midst of this progression as the unity between the fractional and the ordinal series.
We need not load ourselves down with all these extra terms. Let us simply regard government as a new body within the State, distinct from the people and from the Sovereign, and standing between them.

The two bodies differ in an essential way: the State exists by itself, while the government exists only through the Sovereign. So the prince’s dominant will is, or should be, nothing but the general will or the law. His force is simply the public force concentrated in his hands, and as soon as he tries to base some absolute, independent act on his own authority, the tie that binds the whole together begins to loosen. Now suppose the prince finally came to have a particular will more active than the will of the Sovereign, and used the public force in his hands to obey that particular will. There would then be, so to speak, two Sovereigns, one rightful and the other actual. The social union would evaporate at once, and the body politic would be dissolved.

Still, for the government to have a true existence and a real life that sets it apart from the body of the State, and for all its members to act together and achieve the purpose it was set up for, it needs a personality of its own, a sensibility shared by its members, and a force and will of its own aimed at preserving it. This separate existence implies assemblies, councils, the power to deliberate and decide, and rights, titles and privileges that belong exclusively to the prince and make the office of magistrate more honorable the more troublesome it is. The difficulty is how to arrange this subordinate whole within the whole so that it never alters the general constitution by asserting itself. It must always keep its own particular force, which exists to help preserve it, distinct from the public force, which exists to preserve the State. In a word, it must always be ready to sacrifice the government to the people, and never the people to the government.

Furthermore, the artificial body of the government is the work of another artificial body, and so has, we might say, only a borrowed and subordinate life. But that does not stop it from acting with more or less vigor or speed, or from being, so to speak, in more or less robust health. And without directly abandoning the purpose it was created for, it may drift away from it by greater or lesser degrees, depending on how it is constituted.

These differences give rise to the various relations the government ought to have with the body of the State, depending on the chance and particular circumstances that shape the State itself. For the government that is best in itself will often become the most harmful, if its relations have shifted to match the defects of the body politic it belongs to.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 2 — The Constituent Principle in the Various Forms of Government
paragraphs: To lay out the general cause of these differences, we need to distinguish government from its principle, just as we distinguished earlier between the State and the Sovereign.

The body of magistrates can have more members or fewer. We said earlier that the relation of the Sovereign to the subjects grows as the people grows more numerous. By a clear analogy, the same holds for the relation of the government to the magistrates.
But the total force of the government is always the State’s force, and so it never varies. The more of it the government spends on its own members, the less it has left for the whole people.
So the more magistrates there are, the weaker the government. Since this principle is fundamental, we must work to make it clear.

In the person of a magistrate we can tell apart three essentially different wills. First, the private will of the individual, which aims only at his own advantage. Second, the common will of the magistrates, which looks solely to the advantage of the prince. We can call it the corporate will; it is general with respect to the government and particular with respect to the State, of which the government is a part. Third, the will of the people, or the sovereign will, which is general both with respect to the State seen as the whole and with respect to the government seen as a part of that whole.

In a perfect act of legislation, the individual or particular will should count for nothing. The corporate will of the government should hold a very minor place. The general or sovereign will should therefore always prevail, and be the sole guide for all the rest.

The natural order, by contrast, works the other way: these different wills grow more active the more concentrated they are. So the general will is always the weakest, the corporate will comes second, and the individual will is the strongest of all. In government, then, each member is first himself, then a magistrate, then a citizen — exactly the reverse of the order the social system requires.

Granting this, suppose the whole government is in the hands of one man. Then the particular will and the corporate will are wholly united, and so the corporate will is at the highest degree of intensity it can reach. But the use made of the force depends on the degree the will reaches, and the absolute force of the government does not vary. It follows that the most active government is that of one man.

Now suppose the opposite: we join the government to the legislative authority, make the Sovereign the prince as well, and make every citizen a magistrate. Then the corporate will, fused with the general will, can be no more active than that will, and it leaves the particular will as strong as it can possibly be. So the government, whose absolute force never changes, sits at the lowest point of its relative force or activity.

These relations are beyond question, and other considerations confirm them further. For instance, each magistrate is more active in his own body than each citizen is in his. So the particular will has far more influence on the acts of the government than on those of the Sovereign, because almost every magistrate has some governmental function, while no citizen, taken singly, exercises any function of Sovereignty. Furthermore, as the State grows bigger, its real force increases, though not in direct proportion to its growth. But if the State stays the same, the number of magistrates can increase without limit and the government gains no greater real force, since its force is the State’s, and the State’s size stays the same. So the relative force or activity of the government decreases, while its absolute or real force cannot increase.

Moreover, it is certain that promptness in carrying out business diminishes as more people are put in charge of it. Where too much is made of prudence, too little is made of fortune; opportunity is let slip, and deliberation causes the loss of its object.

I have just shown that the government grows slack as the number of magistrates increases, and I showed earlier that the more numerous the people, the greater the repressive force must be. It follows that the relation of the magistrates to the government should vary inversely to the relation of the subjects to the Sovereign. That is, the larger the State, the tighter its government should be, so that the number of rulers shrinks as the number of the people grows.

I should add that I am speaking here of the government’s relative strength, not of how upright it is. On that point the reverse holds: the more numerous the magistracy, the closer the corporate will comes to the general will, while under a single magistrate the corporate will is, as I said, merely a particular will. So what is gained on one side is lost on the other. The art of the legislator is to know where to set the point at which the force and the will of the government, which are always in inverse proportion, meet in the relation that serves the State best.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 3 — The Division of Governments
paragraphs: The last chapter showed what causes the various kinds or forms of government to be distinguished by the number of their members. This chapter has to show how the division is made.

First, the Sovereign may place the government in the hands of the whole people, or of most of them, so that there are more citizens who are magistrates than citizens who are mere private individuals. This form of government is called _democracy_.
Or the Sovereign may confine the government to a few, so that private citizens outnumber magistrates. This form is called _aristocracy_.
Finally, the Sovereign may place the whole government in a single magistrate, from whom all the others get their power. This third form is the commonest. It is called _monarchy_, or royal government.

Notice that all these forms, or at least the first two, come in degrees and can differ very widely. Democracy can take in the whole people or only half of it. Aristocracy, in its turn, can shrink steadily from half the people down to the smallest possible number. Even royalty can be shared to some extent. Sparta always had two kings, as its constitution provided, and the Roman Empire had as many as eight emperors at once, yet no one could say the Empire was split up. So there is a point where each form of government shades into the next, and it becomes clear that, under three broad names, government can really take as many different forms as the State has citizens.

There are still more. Government can also, in some respects, be divided into other parts, one run in one way and one in another. Combining the three forms can then produce a multitude of mixed forms, and each of these can be multiplied by all the simple forms.
There has always been much dispute about the best form of government, without anyone considering that each is the best in some cases and the worst in others.

If the number of supreme magistrates in each State should stand in inverse ratio to the number of citizens, it follows that, in general, democratic government suits small States, aristocratic government suits middle-sized ones, and monarchy suits great ones. This rule follows directly from the principle laid down. But the countless circumstances that may produce exceptions cannot be counted.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 4 — Democracy
paragraphs: The one who makes the law knows better than anyone how it should be carried out and interpreted. It seems, then, that no constitution could be better than one in which the executive and legislative powers are united. Yet this very fact makes such a government inadequate in certain respects, because things that ought to be kept distinct are confused, and the prince and the Sovereign, being the same person, form, so to speak, nothing more than a government without a government.

It is not good for the person who makes the laws to carry them out, nor for the people as a whole to look away from the general view and fix on particular matters. Nothing is more dangerous than private interests influencing public affairs. When the government abuses the laws, the harm is smaller than when the legislator is corrupted, which is the sure result of taking a particular view. Then the State is changed in its very substance, and no reform is possible. A people that never misused the powers of government would never misuse independence; a people that always governed well would not need to be governed.

Taken strictly, the word democracy describes something that has never existed and never will. It goes against the natural order for the many to govern and the few to be governed. We cannot imagine the people staying permanently in session to handle public affairs, and plainly they cannot appoint commissions to do it for them without changing the form of the administration.

In fact, I can state it confidently as a principle: when several bodies share the work of government, the smaller ones sooner or later gain the most authority, if only because they can get business done quickly, so power naturally ends up in their hands.

Besides, such a government assumes so many conditions that are hard to find together! First, a very small State, where the people are easy to assemble and every citizen can readily know all the others. Second, very simple manners, so that business does not pile up and raise thorny problems. Third, a large degree of equality in rank and fortune, since without it equality of rights and authority cannot last. Last, little or no luxury, because luxury comes either from riches or makes them necessary. It corrupts rich and poor together, the rich by owning and the poor by coveting. It sells the country to softness and vanity, and robs the State of all its citizens, making them slaves to one another and all of them slaves to public opinion.

This is why a famous writer made virtue the fundamental principle of Republics, since none of these conditions could exist without it. But that great thinker did not draw the necessary distinctions, so he was often inexact and sometimes obscure. He did not see that sovereign authority is the same everywhere, and so the same principle must be found in every well-constituted State, to a greater or lesser degree, it is true, depending on the form of government.

I would add that no government is so liable to civil wars and internal upheaval as democratic or popular government. None tends so strongly and so constantly to turn into some other form, and none, as it stands, needs more vigilance and courage to keep going. Under such a constitution above all, the citizen should arm himself with strength and steadfastness, and repeat every day of his life what a virtuous Count Palatine[1] said in the Diet of Poland: Malo periculosam libertatem quam quietum servitium.
A people of gods would govern itself democratically. A government so perfect does not suit men.
Lorraine. I prefer liberty with danger to peace with slavery.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 5 — Aristocracy
paragraphs: Here we have two quite separate moral persons, the government and the Sovereign, and so two general wills: one that is general toward all the citizens, and one that is general only for the members of the administration. The government may arrange its internal policy as it likes, but it can never address the people except in the name of the Sovereign, that is, in the name of the people itself. This must never be forgotten.

The earliest societies governed themselves by aristocracy. Heads of families consulted together about public affairs, and the young yielded readily to the authority of experience. Hence names like _priests, elders, senate_, and _gerontes_. The savages of North America still govern themselves in this way, and their government is admirable.

But as the artificial inequality produced by institutions came to outweigh natural inequality, riches or power[1] were put before age, and aristocracy became elective. Finally, the father’s power passed to his children along with his goods, which created patrician families and made government hereditary, and there came to be senators of twenty.

So there are three kinds of aristocracy: natural, elective and hereditary. The first is fit only for simple peoples. The third is the worst of all governments. The second is the best, and it is aristocracy in the proper sense.

Besides the advantage of separating the two powers, this form has another: its members are chosen. In popular government every citizen is born a magistrate, but here only a few hold the magistracy, and they get it only by election.[2] In this way honesty, intelligence, experience and every other claim to rank and public esteem become further guarantees of wise government.

Assemblies, furthermore, are easier to convene. Business is better debated and is carried out with more order and diligence. And venerable senators uphold the State’s credit abroad better than an unknown or despised multitude can.

In short, it is the best and most natural arrangement for the wisest to rule the many, so long as we can be sure they will rule for the benefit of the many and not for themselves. There is no need to multiply instruments, or to employ twenty thousand men to do what a hundred chosen men can do better still. But we must remember that here the interest of the governing body starts to direct the public power less under the guidance of the general will, and that a further unavoidable tendency strips the laws of part of the executive power.

If we ask what is desirable in a given case, the State should not be so small, nor the people so simple and honest, that the laws are carried out directly by the public will, as in a good democracy. Neither should the nation be so large that its rulers must disperse to govern it, and can each play the Sovereign in his own department, starting by making themselves independent and finishing as masters.

But although aristocracy does not require all the virtues that popular government needs, it requires some of its own. One is moderation among the rich, another is contentment among the poor. Complete equality, it seems, would be out of place here, since it was not found even at Sparta.

Furthermore, this form of government brings some inequality of fortune, and that is justified because it lets public affairs usually be handed to those best able to give them all their time. It is not justified, as Aristotle maintains, by the aim of always putting the rich first. On the contrary, it matters that now and then the people choose the other way, and learn that a man’s merit is a stronger claim to rank than wealth.

If the choice is left to the prince’s discretion, it is impossible to avoid sliding into hereditary aristocracy, as the Republics of Venice and Berne in fact did. The first has therefore long been a State in dissolution; the second survives through the extreme wisdom of its senate, and stands as an honorable but highly dangerous exception.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 6 — Monarchy
paragraphs: So far we have looked at the prince as a moral and collective person, made one by the force of the laws and holding executive power in the State. Now we must look at that power when it is gathered into the hands of a natural person, a real man, who alone has the right to dispose of it according to the laws. Such a person is called a monarch or king.

In the other forms of administration, a collective being stands in for an individual. In this form, an individual stands in for a collective being. So the moral unity that made up the prince is also a physical unity, and every quality that the law can bring together only with difficulty in the other forms is found here naturally united.

Thus the will of the people, the will of the prince, the public force of the State and the particular force of the government all respond to one motive power. All the springs of the machine are in the same hands and the whole thing moves toward a single end. Nothing pulls in opposite directions to cancel out the rest, and no constitution can be imagined in which less effort yields more action. Archimedes, sitting calmly on the shore and effortlessly floating a great ship, stands in my mind for a skillful monarch, governing vast states from his study and moving everything while he seems not to move himself.

But although no government is more vigorous, none gives the particular will more sway or lets it dominate the rest more easily. True, everything moves toward the same end, but that end is certainly not the public happiness, and the very strength of the administration keeps working to the State’s harm.

Kings want to be absolute, and people keep calling out to them from a distance that the best way to be absolute is to make themselves loved by their people. That advice is all very well, and in some respects even quite true. Unfortunately, courts will always laugh at it. The power that comes from a people’s love is certainly the greatest, but it is precarious and comes with conditions, and princes will never settle for it. The best kings want to be able to be wicked if they please, and still keep their mastery. Political preachers can tell them as long as they like that the people’s strength is their own, so their first interest is for the people to be prosperous, numerous and formidable. Kings know perfectly well this is untrue. Their first personal interest is for the people to be weak, wretched and unable to resist them. I admit that if the subjects always stayed submissive, it would indeed be in the prince’s interest for the people to be powerful, since its power, being his own, would make him feared by his neighbors. But that interest is only secondary and subordinate, and strength cannot go together with submission. So princes naturally always favor whatever serves their immediate advantage more. This is what Samuel pressed on the Hebrews, and what Machiavelli has plainly shown. He pretended to teach kings, but it was the people he really taught. His _Prince_ is the book of Republicans.[1]

We found on general grounds that monarchy suits only large States, and examining it in itself confirms this. The more people the public administration includes, the smaller the ratio between prince and subjects, and the closer it comes to equality. In democracy the ratio is one, that is, absolute equality. As the government is reduced in numbers, the ratio grows, and it reaches its _maximum_ when government is in the hands of a single person. The distance between prince and people is then too great, and the State has no bond holding it together. To form that bond there must be intermediate ranks, and princes, great personages and nobility to fill them. None of this suits a small State, which is ruined by any class difference.
Yet if it is hard to govern a great State well, it is far harder for one man to do it. And everyone knows what happens when kings put substitutes in their place.

There is an essential and unavoidable defect that will always put monarchical government below republican: in a republic the public voice almost never lifts to the highest offices anyone who is not enlightened and capable, and fit to do them credit. In monarchies, those who reach the top are mostly petty blunderers, petty swindlers and petty intriguers. Their petty talents win them the highest places at Court, and once they are there, serve only to show the public how incompetent they are. The people errs far less often in its choice than the prince does, and a man of real worth among a king’s ministers is almost as rare as a fool at the head of a republican government. So when, by some lucky chance, one of these born governors takes the helm of a monarchy that has nearly been swamped by swarms of “gentlemanly” administrators, everyone is amazed at the resources he turns up, and his arrival marks an era in his country’s history.

For a monarchy to have any chance of being well governed, its population and size must suit the abilities of its governor. Conquering is easier than ruling. With a long enough lever, one finger could move the world; holding it up takes the shoulders of Hercules. However small a State may be, the prince is almost never large enough for it. In the opposite case, where the State happens to be too small for its ruler (which is rare), it is still badly governed. The ruler, forever pursuing his grand designs, forgets the people’s interests, and by misusing the talents he has makes the people just as wretched as a lesser ruler would by lacking the talents he does not have. A kingdom ought, so to speak, to grow or shrink with each reign, according to the prince’s capacity. A senate’s abilities, however, vary less, so under a senate the State can keep fixed frontiers without the administration suffering.

The drawback felt most in monarchical government is the absence of continuous succession, which in the other two forms gives an unbroken link between one ruler and the next. When a king dies, another is needed. Elections leave dangerous gaps and are stormy. Unless the citizens are disinterested and upright to a degree seldom found under this kind of government, intrigue and corruption flourish. The man to whom the State has been sold can hardly avoid selling it in turn, and repaying himself, at the expense of the weak, for the money the powerful have squeezed out of him. Under such an administration, venality sooner or later spreads everywhere, and the peace people enjoy under a king is worse than the disorder of an interregnum.

What has been done to prevent these evils? Crowns have been made hereditary in certain families, and a line of succession has been fixed, so that no disputes arise when kings die. In other words, the drawbacks of regency have been exchanged for those of election, an appearance of calm has been preferred to wise administration, and men have decided it is better to risk having children, monsters or imbeciles for rulers than to argue over choosing good kings. No one has considered that by accepting this risk we are setting nearly all the odds against ourselves. The younger Dionysius answered sensibly when his father scolded him for a shameful act and asked, “Did I set you the example?” “No,” said the son, “but your father was not a king.”

Everything works together to rob a man set in authority over others of any sense of justice and reason. We are told that great effort goes into teaching young princes the art of reigning, but the teaching seems to do them no good. It would be better to begin by teaching them the art of obeying. The greatest kings that history praises were not brought up to reign. Reigning is a science we are farthest from mastering when we have studied too much of it, and we learn it better by obeying than by commanding. “Nam utilissimus idem ac brevissimus bonarum malarumque rerum delectus cogitare quid aut nolueris sub alio principe, aut volueris.”[2]

One consequence of this lack of coherence is that royal government is inconsistent. It is run on one plan and then another, depending on the character of the reigning prince or of those who reign in his name, and so it can never hold a fixed aim or a steady policy for long. This changeability is not found in other forms of government, where the prince is always the same, and it sends the State drifting from principle to principle and project to project. We may say, then, that in general a court is more skilled in intrigue, a senate wiser, and Republics move toward their goals by steadier and better considered policies. Every upheaval in a royal ministry, meanwhile, brings an upheaval in the State, because the one principle shared by all ministers and nearly all kings is to do the opposite, in every respect, of what their predecessors did.

This incoherence also exposes a sophism very familiar to royalist writers on politics. They not only compare civil government to the running of a household, and the prince to a father of a family (an error already refuted), but also freely credit the prince with every virtue he ought to have, and assume he is always what he should be. Grant that assumption, and royal government is plainly better than any other, since it is beyond dispute the strongest, and to be the best as well it needs only a corporate will more in line with the general will.

But if, as Plato[3] says, the “king by nature” is so rare, how often will nature and fortune combine to put a crown on his head? And if a royal education necessarily corrupts those who receive it, what can we hope from a line of men brought up to reign? It is, then, willful self-deception to confuse royal government with the government of a good king. To see royal government as it truly is, we must look at it under incompetent or wicked princes, since either they will arrive on the throne wicked or incompetent, or the throne will make them so.

Our writers have not missed these difficulties, but they are not bothered by them. The cure, they say, is to obey without complaint: God sends bad kings in His anger, and they must be endured as the scourges of Heaven. Talk like this is no doubt edifying, but it belongs in a pulpit rather than a book on politics. What should we think of a doctor who promises miracles, and whose whole skill lies in urging the patient to be patient? We know perfectly well that we must put up with a bad government once we have one. The question is how to find a good one.

And the contradiction between the teaching of the _Prince_ and that of the _Discourses on Livy_ and the _History of Florence_ shows that this deep political thinker has so far been read only by shallow or corrupt readers. chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 7 — Mixed Governments
paragraphs: Strictly speaking, no government is simple. A lone ruler still needs subordinate magistrates, and a popular government still needs a head. So in the way executive power is shared out, there is always a gradation from the greater number to the lesser. The difference is that sometimes the many depend on the few, and sometimes the few on the many.

Sometimes the power is divided equally. This happens either when the parts depend on one another, as in the government of England, or when each part is independent of the others but its authority is incomplete, as in Poland. This last form is bad, because it gives the government no unity and leaves the State without a bond to hold it together.
Is a simple government or a mixed one better? Political writers argue over this question endlessly. It has to be answered the same way we answered the earlier question about all forms of government.

Simple government is better in itself, precisely because it is simple. But when the executive power does not depend enough on the legislative power — _i.e._ when the prince is more closely tied to the Sovereign than the people are to the prince — this imbalance must be corrected by dividing the government. For then all the parts have just as much authority over the subjects, while their division makes them, taken together, less strong against the Sovereign.

The same disadvantage can also be prevented by appointing intermediate magistrates. They leave the government whole, and serve only to balance the two powers and maintain their respective rights. The government is then not mixed but moderated.

The opposite problem can be cured in a similar way: when the government is too lax, tribunals can be set up to concentrate it. This is done in all democracies. In the first case the government is divided to make it weak, in the second to make it strong. The highest degrees of both strength and weakness are found in simple governments, while mixed forms give a middling strength.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 8 — That All Forms of Government Do Not Suit All Countries
paragraphs: Liberty is not the fruit of every climate, so it is not within reach of every people. The more one considers this principle, laid down by Montesquieu, the truer it seems; the more it is attacked, the more chances it gets to be confirmed by new proofs.

In every government that exists, the public person consumes without producing. Where, then, does it get what it consumes? From the labor of its members. The needs of the public are supplied out of the surplus of individuals. It follows that the civil State can survive only as long as people’s labor yields them more than they need.

The size of this surplus is not the same in every country. In some it is large, in others middling, in others zero, and in some even negative. The relation between product and subsistence depends on how fertile the climate is, what kind of work the land demands, what its products are like, how strong its inhabitants are, how much or how little they find they need to consume, and several other factors that together make up the whole relation.

On the other hand, governments are not all of one nature: some devour more than others, and the differences between them rest on this second principle, that the farther public contributions travel from their source, the heavier they weigh.

The burden should be measured not by the amount of the taxes but by the path they must travel to get back to those they came from. When the circulation is quick and well established, it does not matter whether the people pay much or little; the people are always rich and, financially speaking, all is well. But if what the people pay does not return to them, however little it is, they are soon exhausted by giving continually. The State is then never rich, and the people are always a people of beggars.

It follows that as the distance between people and government grows, tribute gets heavier. So in a democracy the people carry the lightest load, in an aristocracy a heavier one, and in a monarchy the heaviest of all. Monarchy therefore suits only wealthy nations, aristocracy States of middling size and wealth, and democracy States that are small and poor.

In fact, the more we reflect, the clearer it becomes what separates free States from monarchical ones. In the former, everything is used for the public advantage. In the latter, the public forces and those of individuals act on each other, and one grows as the other weakens. Finally, instead of governing subjects to make them happy, despotism makes them wretched so that it can govern them.
We find, then, in every climate, natural causes from which we can determine the form of government that the climate requires, and we can even say what kind of inhabitants it should have.

Unfriendly, barren land, where the product does not repay the work, should stay desert and uncultivated, or be settled only by savages. Land where people’s work yields just the bare _minimum_ needed to live should be inhabited by barbarous peoples; in such places no polity is possible. Land where the surplus of product over work is only middling suits free peoples. Land where the soil is rich and fertile and gives a great product for little work calls for monarchical government, so that the prince’s luxury can consume the surplus the subjects have beyond their needs; for it is better that the government absorb this excess than that individuals squander it. I know there are exceptions. But the exceptions themselves confirm the rule, because sooner or later they produce revolutions that put things back in their natural order.

General laws must always be kept apart from the individual causes that can modify their effects. Suppose the whole South were covered with Republics and the whole North with despotic States. It would still be true that, where climate is concerned, despotism suits hot countries, barbarism cold ones, and good polity temperate regions. I also see that even with the principle granted, people may dispute how to apply it. They may say that some cold countries are very fertile and some tropical ones very unproductive. But this difficulty exists only for those who do not look at the question from every side. As I have already said, we must take into account labor, strength, consumption and so on.

Take two tracts of land of equal extent, one producing five and the other ten. Suppose the inhabitants of the first consume four and those of the second nine. The first then has a surplus of one fifth and the second a surplus of one tenth. The ratio of the two surpluses is the reverse of the ratio of the products, and the tract producing only five yields twice the surplus of the tract producing ten.

But nobody is talking about a double product, and I do not think anyone would, as a general rule, rank the fertility of cold countries equal to that of hot ones. Let us suppose, though, that they are equal. Let us say, if you like, that England stands level with Sicily and Poland with Egypt; further south we get Africa and the Indies, and further north nothing at all. To get that equal product, what a difference there must be in the tillage! In Sicily you only have to scratch the ground; in England, how men must toil! And where more hands are needed to get the same product, the surplus has to be smaller.

Consider also that the same number of men eat far less in hot countries. The climate demands moderation for the sake of health, and Europeans who try to live there as they do at home all die of dysentery and indigestion. “Compared with the Asiatics,” says Chardin, “we are carnivorous animals, wolves. Some put the sobriety of the Persians down to their country being less cultivated. I believe instead that their country produces fewer goods because the inhabitants need less. If their frugality,” he goes on, “came from the barrenness of the land, only the poor would eat little, but everybody does. Besides, people would eat more or less in different provinces according to the land’s fertility, yet the same sobriety is found all through the kingdom. They are very proud of their way of living. They say you only have to look at their complexion to see how far it surpasses that of the Christians. And indeed the Persians have an even complexion, with skin that is fair, fine and smooth, while their subjects the Armenians, who live in the European way, have a rough, blotchy complexion and heavy, clumsy bodies.”

The nearer you get to the equator, the less people live on. They barely touch meat; their ordinary food is rice, maize, curcur, millet and cassava. In the Indies there are millions of men whose food costs less than a halfpenny a day. Even in Europe, Northern and Southern peoples differ considerably in appetite. A Spaniard can live for a week on a German’s dinner. In the countries where men have bigger appetites, luxury therefore takes the form of consumption. In England luxury means a well-filled table; in Italy you feast on sugar and flowers.

Luxury in clothing shows the same differences. Where the seasons change swiftly and violently, men wear clothes that are better and plainer. Where people dress only for show, they care more about what catches the eye than about what is useful, and the clothes themselves become a luxury. In Naples you can see men walking every day in the Pausilippeum in gold-embroidered upper garments and nothing else. Buildings are the same: where there is nothing to fear from the weather, magnificence is the only consideration. In Paris and London you want to be housed warmly and comfortably; in Madrid you have superb salons but not a window that closes, and you go to bed in a mere hole.

In hot countries food is far more substantial and succulent, and this third difference cannot help affecting the second. Why are so many vegetables eaten in Italy? Because there they are good, nourishing and excellent in taste. In France they are raised on nothing but water, so they are far from nourishing and count for nothing at table. All the same, they take up just as much ground and cost at least as much effort to grow. It is a proven fact that Barbary wheat, though inferior to French wheat in other respects, yields much more flour, and that French wheat in turn yields more than wheat from the northern countries. From this we may infer that a similar gradation in the same direction, from equator to pole, holds generally. But is it not an obvious disadvantage for an equal product to contain less nourishment?

One more point can be added, which both rests on these and strengthens them. Hot countries need fewer inhabitants than cold ones, and can feed more of them. So there is a double surplus, all of it to the advantage of despotism. The larger the territory a given number of inhabitants occupies, the harder revolt becomes, because quick or secret concerted action is impossible, and the government can easily expose plots and cut off communications. But the more a numerous people is packed together, the less the government can usurp the Sovereign’s place. The people’s leaders can deliberate as safely in their houses as the prince in council, and the crowd can assemble in the squares as quickly as the prince’s troops in their quarters. The advantage of tyrannical government therefore lies in acting across great distances. With the help of the rallying-points it sets up, its strength, like that of the lever,[1] grows with distance. The strength of the people, by contrast, acts only when concentrated. Spread out, it evaporates and is lost, like powder scattered on the ground, which catches fire only grain by grain. The least populous countries are therefore the best suited to tyranny: fierce animals rule only in deserts.

Its scattered members serve it as rallying-points for acting against the people at a distance, but it has no rallying-point for acting directly on those members themselves. So the length of the lever is its weakness in the one case and its strength in the other.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 9 — The Marks of a Good Government
paragraphs: The question “What is the best government, absolutely?” has no answer, and is also indeterminate. Or rather, there are as many good answers as there are possible combinations of the absolute and relative situations of all nations.
But if we ask by what sign we can tell whether a given people is governed well or badly, that is a different matter. It is a question of fact, so it can be answered.

Yet it goes unanswered, because everyone wants to answer it his own way. Subjects praise public tranquility, citizens individual liberty. One group prefers security of property, the other security of person. One thinks the best government is the strictest, the other that the mildest is best. One wants crimes punished, the other wants them prevented. One wants the State feared by its neighbors, the other wants it overlooked. One is satisfied if money circulates, the other demands that the people have bread. Even if people agreed on these points and others like them, would we be any further along? Moral qualities cannot be measured exactly, so agreeing on the mark does not mean agreeing on its value.

For my part, I am constantly amazed that so simple a mark goes unrecognized, or that people are so dishonest as to refuse to admit it. What is the purpose of political association? The preservation and prosperity of its members. And what is the surest sign that they are preserved and prosperous? Their numbers and population. So look nowhere else for this disputed mark. All else being equal, the government under which the citizens multiply most, without outside help, naturalization or colonies, is beyond question the best. The government under which a people shrinks and dwindles is the worst. Calculators, it is for you to count, to measure, to compare.[1]

the preference for human prosperity. Those in which letters and the arts have flourished have been admired too much, because nobody has seen through the hidden purpose of their cultivation or counted its fatal effects. “Idque apud imperitos humanitas vocabatur, cum pars servitutis esset.” [“Fools called ‘humanity’ what was a part of slavery,” Tacitus, _Agricola_, 31.] Shall we never see, in the maxims that books lay down, the vulgar self-interest that makes their authors speak? No. Whatever they say, when a country loses population, however famous it is, it is not true that all is well; and it is not enough for a poet to have an income of 100,000 francs to make his age the best of all. We should look less at the apparent calm and tranquility of the rulers than at the well-being of nations as wholes, and above all of the most populous States. A hailstorm lays waste several cantons, but it seldom causes a famine. Uprisings and civil wars give rulers rude shocks, but they are not the real ills of peoples, who may even get a breathing space while others dispute who will tyrannize over them. A people’s true prosperity and calamities come from its permanent condition. It is when the whole remains crushed under the yoke that decay sets in, and the rulers can destroy the people at will; “ubi solitudinem faciunt, pacem appellant.” [“Where they create solitude, they call it peace,” Tacitus, _Agricola_, 31.] When the quarrels of the great troubled the kingdom of France, and the Coadjutor of Paris took a dagger in his pocket to the Parliament, the people of France went on prospering and multiplying in dignity, ease and freedom. Long ago Greece flourished in the midst of the most savage wars; blood ran in torrents, and yet the whole country was full of inhabitants. It seemed, says Machiavelli, that in the midst of murder, proscription and civil war our republic only thrived: the virtue, morals and independence of its citizens did more to strengthen it than all their dissensions did to weaken it. A little disturbance gives the soul elasticity; what makes the race truly prosperous is not so much peace as liberty.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 10 — The Abuse of Government and Its Tendency to Degenerate
paragraphs: The particular will is always working against the general will, so the government is always straining against sovereignty. The harder it strains, the more the constitution changes. And because there is no other corporate will here to create a balance by resisting the will of the prince, sooner or later the prince must inevitably suppress the Sovereign and break the social compact. This defect is unavoidable and built in. From the very birth of the body politic it works ceaselessly to destroy it, just as old age and death end up destroying the human body.
Government degenerates by two general routes, _i.e._ when it contracts and when the State is dissolved.

Government contracts when it passes from the many to the few, that is, from democracy to aristocracy and from aristocracy to royalty. Contracting is its natural propensity.[1] If it went the other way, from the few to the many, it could be called relaxed; but this reverse order is impossible.

Indeed, governments change their form only when their energy is spent and leaves them too weak to hold on to what they have. If a government both widened its sphere and loosened its grip, its force would drop to nothing and it would survive even less. So the spring has to be wound up and the grip tightened as it slackens; otherwise the State that rests on it will come to ruin.
The State can be dissolved in either of two ways.

The first is when the prince stops administering the State according to the laws and usurps the sovereign power. A remarkable change then takes place: it is not the government but the State that contracts. I mean that the great State is dissolved and another is formed inside it, made up only of the members of the government, and for the rest of the people this new State is nothing but master and tyrant. So at the moment the government usurps sovereignty, the social compact is broken, and all private citizens recover their natural liberty by right, and are forced to obey but not bound.

The same happens when the members of the government each separately usurp the power they ought to exercise only as a body. This breaks the laws just as badly and causes even greater disorder. There are then, so to speak, as many princes as there are magistrates, and the State, divided just as the government is, either perishes or changes its form.

Once the State is dissolved, the abuse of government, whatever form it takes, goes by the common name of _anarchy_. To be more precise: democracy degenerates into _ochlocracy_, aristocracy into _oligarchy_, and I would add that royalty degenerates into _tyranny_. This last word, however, is ambiguous and needs explaining.

In everyday speech, a tyrant is a king who governs with violence and with no regard for justice and law. In the exact sense, a tyrant is a private individual who takes royal authority for himself without any right to it. The Greeks understood the word this way: they used “tyrant” without distinction for good and bad princes alike, whenever their authority was not legitimate.[2] _Tyrant_ and _usurper_ are thus perfectly synonymous terms.

So that I can give different things different names, I call the person who usurps royal authority a _tyrant_ and the person who usurps sovereign power a _despot_. The tyrant forces his way in against the laws in order to govern according to the laws; the despot puts himself above the laws themselves. So the tyrant cannot be a despot, but the despot is always a tyrant.

It is most astonishing that after more than twelve hundred years of existence the Venetians still seem to be at the second stage, which they reached with the _Serrar di Consiglio_ in 1198. As for the ancient Dukes that people cite against this, it has been proved, whatever the _Squittinio della libertà veneta_ may say about them, that they were never Sovereigns in any sense.

The case certain to be cited against my view is the Roman Republic. It will be said that Rome took exactly the opposite course, passing from monarchy to aristocracy and from aristocracy to democracy. I do not see it that way at all.

What Romulus first set up was a mixed government, which soon sank into despotism. For particular reasons the State died before its time, the way newborn children sometimes die before reaching manhood. The expulsion of the Tarquins was the real birth of the Republic. But at first it took no lasting form, because by not abolishing the patriciate it left half its work undone. That left hereditary aristocracy, the worst of all legitimate forms of administration, in conflict with democracy, and the form of the government was not settled until the tribunate was established, as Machiavelli has shown. Only then was there a true government and a genuine democracy. In fact, the people were then not only Sovereign but also magistrate and judge. The senate was only a subordinate tribunal, there to temper and concentrate the government. And the consuls, though they were patricians, first magistrates and absolute generals in war, were in Rome itself no more than presidents of the people.

From then on the government followed its natural tendency and leaned strongly toward aristocracy. The patriciate, we may say, abolished itself. The aristocracy was no longer found in the body of patricians, as at Venice and Genoa, but in the senate, which consisted of patricians and plebeians, and even in the body of tribunes once they began to take on an active function. Names do not alter facts, and when a people has rulers who govern for it, the government is an aristocracy, whatever name they bear.

Abuse of aristocracy led to the civil wars and the triumvirate. Sulla, Julius Caesar and Augustus became in fact real monarchs, and finally, under the despotism of Tiberius, the State was dissolved. Roman history thus confirms the principle I have laid down, rather than disproving it.
