[All those are called and considered tyrants who hold perpetual power in a State that has known liberty.] Aristotle (_Nicomachean Ethics_, Book viii, chapter x) does, it is true, distinguish the tyrant from the king by saying that the former governs in his own interest and the latter only for the good of his subjects. But all Greek authors in general used the word _tyrant_ in a different sense, as Xenophon’s _Hiero_ shows most clearly; and Aristotle’s distinction would also imply that from the very beginning of the world there has never yet been a single king.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 11 — The Death of the Body Politic
paragraphs: This is the natural and unavoidable direction of even the best constituted governments. Sparta and Rome both perished, so what State can hope to last forever? If we want to build a government that endures a long time, we should not even dream of making it eternal. To succeed, we must not attempt the impossible, and we must not flatter ourselves that we can give a human creation a stability that the human condition does not allow.

The body politic, like the human body, starts dying the moment it is born, and carries the causes of its own destruction inside it. But either one may have a sturdier constitution, better suited to keep it alive for a shorter or longer time. A man’s constitution is the work of nature; the State’s is the work of art. People cannot extend their own lives, but it is up to them to extend the life of the State as far as they can, by giving it the best possible constitution. Even the best constituted State will end; but it will end later than any other, unless some unforeseen accident destroys it before its time.

The body politic draws its life from the sovereign authority. The legislative power is the heart of the State; the executive power is its brain, which sets every part moving. The brain can be paralyzed and the person still live. A man can remain feeble-minded and go on living; but once the heart stops doing its work, the animal is dead.

The State survives not through its laws but through the legislative power. A law made yesterday does not bind us today. But silence is taken as tacit consent, and the Sovereign is held to be confirming, at every moment, the laws it could repeal and does not. Whatever it has once declared that it wills, it goes on willing, unless it revokes the declaration.

Why, then, do we show so much respect for old laws? For this very reason. We have to believe that only the excellence of the old acts of will could have kept them alive so long: had the Sovereign not found them wholly beneficial, it would have revoked them a thousand times. So in any well constituted State the laws do not weaken; they keep gaining strength, because the precedent of age makes them more venerable every day. But wherever laws grow weak as they grow old, that proves there is no longer a legislative power, and that the State is dead.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 12 — How the Sovereign Authority Maintains Itself
paragraphs: The Sovereign has no force except the legislative power, so it acts only through the laws. The laws are nothing but the authentic acts of the general will, so the Sovereign can act only when the people is assembled. A people in assembly, I shall be told, is a mere fantasy. Today it is. Two thousand years ago it was not. Has human nature changed?

In moral matters, what is possible has narrower limits than we imagine only because of our weaknesses, our vices and our prejudices, which hem it in. Base souls do not believe in great men; vile slaves sneer at the very name of liberty.

Let us judge what can be done by looking at what has been done. I shall say nothing of the Republics of ancient Greece. But in my view the Roman Republic was a great State, and Rome a great city. The last census found four hundred thousand citizens in Rome able to bear arms, and the last count of the Empire’s population came to over four million citizens, not counting subjects, foreigners, women, children and slaves.

One might suppose there would be endless difficulties in gathering the vast population of that capital and its surroundings so often. Yet hardly a few weeks went by without the Roman people meeting in assembly, and often more than once. They exercised not only the rights of Sovereignty but part of those of government as well. They dealt with certain matters and judged certain cases, and this whole people was found in the public meeting-place almost as often as magistrates as it was as citizens.

If we went back to the earliest history of nations, we would find that most ancient governments, even monarchies such as the Macedonian and the Frankish, held similar councils. In any case, the one undeniable fact I have given answers every objection; to reason from what has actually happened to what is possible is sound logic.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 13 — The Same (continued)
paragraphs: It is not enough that the assembled people once fixed the constitution of the State by approving a body of law. It is not enough that they once set up a perpetual government, or settled the election of magistrates once and for all. Unforeseen circumstances may call for extraordinary assemblies, but beyond those there must be regular assemblies at fixed times, which no one can abolish or postpone. Then on the proper day the law itself calls the people together, and no formal summons is needed.

But apart from these assemblies that are authorized by their date alone, any assembly of the people that the appointed magistrates have not summoned, in the prescribed forms, should be regarded as unlawful, and everything it does as null and void, because the order to assemble should itself come from the law.

How often lawful assemblies should meet depends on too many considerations for any exact rule to be given. All that can be said in general is that the stronger the government, the more often the Sovereign should appear.

That may work for a single city, I shall be told; but what happens when the State contains several? Must the sovereign authority be split up? Or must it be gathered into one city, with all the rest made subject to it?

Neither, I reply. First, the sovereign authority is one and simple, and it cannot be divided without being destroyed. Second, no city can legitimately be made subject to another, any more than one nation can, because the essence of the body politic lies in reconciling obedience with liberty. The words subject and Sovereign are exactly matching correlatives, and their meaning comes together in the single word “citizen.”

I answer further that uniting several cities into one city is always bad, and that anyone who wants such a union should not expect to escape its natural disadvantages. It is pointless to raise the abuses of great States against someone who wants only small ones. But how can small States be given the strength to resist great ones, as the Greek cities once resisted the Great King, and as Holland and Switzerland more recently resisted the House of Austria?

Nevertheless, if the State cannot be reduced to its right size, one resource still remains: to allow no capital, to make the seat of government move from city to city, and to have the Provincial Estates of the country meet in each city in turn.

Spread the population evenly over the territory, give everyone everywhere the same rights, and bring abundance and life to every corner of it. In this way the State will become as strong and as well governed as it can be. Remember that city walls are built out of the ruins of country houses. For every palace I see rising in the capital, I see in my mind’s eye a whole countryside laid waste.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 14 — The Same (continued)
paragraphs: The moment the people is lawfully assembled as a sovereign body, the government loses all jurisdiction and the executive power is suspended. The person of the humblest citizen becomes as sacred and inviolable as that of the first magistrate, for where the person represented is present, there are no representatives. Most of the tumults in the Roman comitia came from ignorance or neglect of this rule. In those assemblies the consuls were merely the presidents of the people, the tribunes were mere speakers,[1] and the senate was nothing at all.

The prince recognizes, or ought to recognize, a real superior during these pauses, and he has always viewed them with alarm. These assemblies of the people are the shield of the body politic and the curb on the government, and rulers have always dreaded them. So they spare no effort, no objection, no difficulty and no promise to keep the citizens from holding them. When the citizens are greedy, cowardly and fainthearted, and love comfort more than liberty, they cannot hold out long against the government’s redoubled efforts. So the resisting force keeps growing, the sovereign authority finally vanishes, and most cities fall and perish before their time.
But sometimes an intermediate power steps in between the sovereign authority and arbitrary government, and something must be said about it.
Parliament. These functions were so similar that they would have set the consuls and the tribunes against each other, even if all jurisdiction had been suspended.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 15 — Deputies or Representatives
paragraphs: Once public service is no longer the citizens’ chief business, and they would rather serve with their money than with their persons, the State is close to falling. When war calls them out, they pay troops and stay home. When the council must meet, they appoint deputies and stay home. Through laziness and money, they end up with soldiers to enslave their country and representatives to sell it.

Personal services turn into money payments because of the bustle of commerce and the arts, the greedy chase after profit, and a soft love of comfort. Men give up part of their profits so they can have leisure to increase them. Make gifts of money, and you will soon be in chains. The word _finance_ is a slavish word, unknown in the city-state. In a truly free country, the citizens do everything with their own hands and nothing with money. Far from paying to be excused from their duties, they would pay for the privilege of doing them themselves. I am far from sharing the common view: I think forced labor is less opposed to liberty than taxes are.

The better a State’s constitution is, the more public affairs outweigh private ones in the citizens’ minds. Private affairs even matter much less, because the sum of the common happiness supplies a larger part of each person’s happiness, and so there is less left for him to look for in his own concerns. In a well-ordered city, every man rushes to the assemblies. Under a bad government, no one will take a step to attend them. No one is interested in what happens there, it is foreseen that the general will will not prevail, and domestic concerns swallow up everything. Good laws lead to better ones, and bad laws bring worse. Once a man says of the State’s affairs _What does it matter to me?_ the State can be given up for lost.

Cooling patriotism, busy private interest, the vast size of States, conquest and the abuse of government gave rise to the idea of deputies or representatives of the people in the national assemblies. In some countries men have dared to call these people the Third Estate. In this arrangement the private interest of two orders comes first and second, and the public interest gets only third place.

Sovereignty cannot be represented, for the same reason that it cannot be given away. It lies essentially in the general will, and a will cannot be represented: it is either itself or something else, with nothing in between. The people’s deputies, therefore, are not and cannot be its representatives. They are only its stewards, and they cannot conclude anything definitively. Any law the people has not ratified in person is null and void — it is not a law at all. The people of England thinks it is free, but it is badly mistaken. It is free only while it elects members of parliament. As soon as they are elected, it is a slave and nothing. The way it uses its brief moments of liberty shows that it deserves to lose them.

The idea of representation is modern. It comes to us from feudal government, that unjust and absurd system that degrades humanity and dishonors the name of man. In ancient republics, and even in monarchies, the people never had representatives, and the word itself was unknown. It is very strange that in Rome, where the tribunes were so sacred, nobody ever imagined they could usurp the functions of the people. Among so great a multitude, they never once tried to pass a plebiscitum on their own authority. Still, we can get an idea of the difficulties a large crowd sometimes caused from what happened in the time of the Gracchi, when some of the citizens had to vote from the rooftops.

Where right and liberty are everything, drawbacks count for nothing. This wise people valued everything at its true worth. It let its lictors do what its tribunes would never have dared attempt, since it never feared that its lictors might try to represent it.

To explain how the tribunes sometimes did represent the people, it is enough to see how the government represents the Sovereign. Law is purely the declaration of the general will, so clearly the people cannot be represented when it exercises the legislative power. The executive power, however, is only the force applied to give the law effect, and there the people can and should be represented. This shows that, looked at closely, very few nations would turn out to have laws. However that may be, the tribunes held no executive power, so they could never represent the Roman people by right of the powers entrusted to them, but only by usurping those of the senate.

In Greece, the people did everything it had to do for itself, and it was constantly gathered in the public square. The Greeks lived in a mild climate and had no natural greed. Slaves did their work, and their great concern was liberty. You do not have these advantages, so how can you keep the same rights? Your harsher climates add to your needs;[1] for half the year your public squares cannot be lived in, and the flat sound of your languages makes them unfit to be heard in the open air. You give up more for profit than for liberty, and you fear poverty more than slavery.

What then? Can liberty be maintained only with the support of slavery? Perhaps so. Extremes meet. Whatever goes against nature has its drawbacks, and civil society has more than anything. There are unhappy circumstances in which we can keep our liberty only at the expense of others, and the citizen can be perfectly free only when the slave is most utterly a slave. Sparta was like that. As for you, modern peoples, you have no slaves, but you are slaves yourselves; you pay for their liberty with your own. You can boast of this preference as you like, but I find more cowardice in it than humanity.

None of this means that we must have slaves, or that the right of slavery is legitimate. I am simply explaining why modern peoples, who believe they are free, have representatives, and why ancient peoples had none. In any case, the moment a people lets itself be represented, it is no longer free, and it no longer exists.

Taking everything into account, I do not see how the Sovereign can go on exercising its rights among us, unless the city is very small. But if the city is very small, will it not be conquered? No. Later I will show how a great people’s[2] strength against outsiders can be combined with the convenient organization and good order of a small State.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 16 — That the Institution of Government Is Not a Contract
paragraphs: Once the legislative power is firmly established, the next task is to establish the executive power in the same way. The executive power works only through particular acts and is not part of the essence of the legislative power, so it is naturally separate from it. If the Sovereign, as such, could hold the executive power, right and fact would be so mixed up that no one could tell what was law and what was not. The body politic would be disfigured, and would soon fall victim to the very violence it was instituted to prevent.

By the social compact the citizens are all equal, so all can prescribe what all should do, but no one has the right to demand that another do what he does not do himself. This is exactly the right, indispensable for giving the body politic life and movement, that the Sovereign gives to the prince when it institutes the government.

Some have maintained that this act of establishment was a contract between the people and the rulers it sets over itself — a contract laying down conditions between the two parties, under which one is bound to command and the other to obey. Everyone will agree, I am sure, that this is a strange sort of contract to make. But let us see whether the view holds up.

First, the supreme authority can no more be altered than it can be transferred: limiting it destroys it. For the Sovereign to put a superior over itself is absurd and contradictory, and to bind itself to obey a master would mean returning to absolute liberty.
Moreover, such a contract between the people and certain persons would clearly be a particular act. It follows that it can be neither a law nor an act of Sovereignty, and so would be illegitimate.

It is plain, too, that in relation to each other the contracting parties would stand under the law of nature alone, with no guarantee at all of their mutual undertakings, which is wholly at odds with the civil state. Whoever commands force can always control how the contract is carried out. So it would come to the same thing to call it a “contract” when one man says to another, “I give you all my goods, on condition that you give me back as much of them as you please.”
There is only one contract in the State, and that is the act of association, which by itself rules out any second contract. No public contract can be conceived that would not violate the first.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 17 — The Institution of Government
paragraphs: What kind of act, in general terms, is the one that institutes government? To begin with, it is a complex act, made up of two others: establishing the law, and carrying it out.
In the first, the Sovereign decrees that a governing body will exist in this or that form. This act is clearly a law.

In the second, the people appoints the rulers who will be put in charge of the government just established. This appointment is a particular act, so it is clearly not a second law. It is only a consequence of the first, and a function of government.

The hard part is understanding how an act of government can happen before any government exists, and how the people, which is nothing but Sovereign or subjects, can in some circumstances become a prince or magistrates.

Here one of the astonishing properties of the body politic shows itself: it can reconcile operations that seem to contradict each other. It does this by suddenly turning sovereignty into democracy. Nothing visibly changes. Through nothing more than a new relation of all to all, the citizens become magistrates, moving from general acts to particular ones, from making law to carrying it out.

This change of relation is no theoretical hair-splitting without examples in practice. It happens every day in the English Parliament. On certain occasions the Lower House turns itself into a Grand Committee, to discuss business more effectively. One moment it is a sovereign court; the next it is a mere commission. It then reports to itself, as the House of Commons, what it did in Grand Committee, and debates all over again under one name what it has already settled under another.

Indeed, democratic government has this special advantage: it can be established in actual fact by a simple act of the general will. After that, the provisional government either stays in power, if that is the form adopted, or else sets up, in the Sovereign’s name, the government that the law prescribes. In this way everything proceeds regularly. There is no other legitimate way to set up a government that is consistent with the principles laid down so far.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 18 — How to Check the Usurpations of Government
paragraphs: What we have just said confirms Chapter XVI and makes it clear that instituting government is not a contract but a law. Those who hold the executive power are not the people’s masters but its officers. The people can appoint them and dismiss them whenever it pleases. For them the question is never one of contract, only of obedience. When they take on the functions the State imposes on them, they are merely doing their duty as citizens, and they have no right at all to argue over the terms.

So when the people sets up a hereditary government, whether a monarchy limited to one family or an aristocracy limited to one class, it is not taking on an obligation. It is giving the administration a provisional form, which stands until the people decides to order it differently.

It is true that such changes are always dangerous, and that an established government should never be disturbed unless it becomes incompatible with the public good. But this caution is a maxim of policy, not a rule of right. The State is no more obliged to leave civil authority with its rulers than to leave military authority with its generals.

It is also true that one cannot be too careful, in such cases, to observe every formality needed to tell a regular, legitimate act apart from a seditious tumult, and the will of a whole people from the clamor of a faction. Here above all, one should grant the unwelcome possibility no more than strict logic forces one to grant. Yet the prince gains a great advantage from this requirement: he can hold on to his power against the people without anyone being able to say he has usurped it. Since he appears to be using only his rights, he easily extends them. Under the pretext of keeping the peace, he prevents the assemblies meant to restore order. He exploits a silence he refuses to let anyone break, and irregularities he causes himself, to presume the backing of those whom fear keeps from speaking, and to punish those who dare to speak. This is how the decemvirs, elected first for one year and then kept in office for a second, tried to make their power permanent by forbidding the comitia to assemble. By this easy method every government in the world, once clothed with public power, sooner or later usurps the sovereign authority.

The periodic assemblies I have already described are meant to prevent or delay this calamity, above all when no formal summons is needed. Then the prince cannot stop them without openly declaring himself a lawbreaker and an enemy of the State.
These assemblies have the sole purpose of maintaining the social compact. They should always open by putting two propositions that cannot be suppressed and that are voted on separately.
The first is: “Is it the Sovereign’s pleasure to keep the present form of government?”
The second is: “Is it the people’s pleasure that those who now hold the administration should keep it?”

Here I am taking for granted what I believe I have shown: the State has no fundamental law that cannot be revoked, not even the social compact itself. If all the citizens assembled and agreed to break the compact, there is no doubt it would be broken quite legitimately. Grotius even holds that each man can renounce his membership in his own State and, on leaving the country, take back his natural liberty and his goods.[1] It would be absurd if all the citizens assembled could not do what each of them can do alone.
and avoid having to serve his country when it is in need. Fleeing in such a case would be a crime, and punishable. It would be desertion, not withdrawal.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 1 — That the General Will Is Indestructible
paragraphs: As long as several men assembled together regard themselves as a single body, they have only one will, which is concerned with their common preservation and general well-being. In that case all the workings of the State are vigorous and simple, and its rules are clear and bright. There are no tangles or conflicts of interest; the common good shows itself plainly everywhere, and only good sense is needed to see it. Peace, unity and equality are the enemies of political subtlety. Upright, simple men are hard to deceive precisely because they are simple: tricks and clever pretexts do not work on them, and they are not even subtle enough to be dupes. When we see bands of peasants, among the happiest people in the world, settling the affairs of State under an oak tree and always acting wisely, can we help despising the refined methods of other nations, which make themselves famous and miserable with so much art and mystery?

A State governed this way needs very few laws. When it becomes necessary to issue new ones, everyone sees the necessity. The first man to propose them merely says what all have already felt. There is no need for factions, intrigues or eloquence to get a law passed that everyone has already resolved to follow, as soon as he is sure the others will do likewise.

Theorists go wrong because they see only States that were badly constituted from the start, and they are struck by how impossible it would be to apply such a policy to them. They have great fun imagining all the absurdities that a clever rascal or a smooth talker could get the people of Paris or London to believe. They do not know that the people of Berne would have put Cromwell to “the bells,” and the Genevese would have put the Duc de Beaufort on the treadmill.

But when the social bond starts to loosen and the State to weaken, when particular interests begin to be felt and smaller societies begin to influence the larger one, the common interest changes and meets opposition. Opinion is no longer unanimous. The general will stops being the will of all. Contradictory views and debates arise, and even the best advice is accepted only after being challenged.

Finally, the State stands on the eve of ruin and keeps up only a vain, illusory, formal existence. The social bond is broken in every heart, and the meanest interest brazenly seizes the sacred name of “public good.” Then the general will falls silent. All men, guided by secret motives, no longer give their views as citizens, any more than if the State had never existed, and unjust decrees aimed solely at private interest are passed under the name of laws.

Does it follow that the general will is destroyed or corrupted? Not at all. It is always constant, unalterable and pure, but it is overridden by other wills that encroach on its territory. Each man, in separating his interest from the common interest, sees clearly that he cannot separate them entirely. But his share in the public misfortunes seems trivial next to the exclusive good he hopes to make his own. Setting aside this particular good, he wills the general good in his own interest as strongly as anyone else. Even when he sells his vote for money, he does not extinguish the general will in himself; he only evades it. His fault is to change the question, and to answer something other than what he is asked. Instead of saying with his vote, “It is to the advantage of the State,” he says, “It is to the advantage of this man or that party that this or that view should win.” So the law of public order in assemblies is less to maintain the general will there than to make sure that the question is always put to it, and that the answer is always given by it.

Here I could set down many reflections on the simple right to vote in every act of Sovereignty — a right no one can take from the citizens — and also on the right to state opinions, make proposals, divide and discuss, which the government is always most careful to leave to its own members alone. But this important subject would need a treatise of its own, and it is impossible to say everything in a single work.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 2 — Voting
paragraphs: The last chapter shows that the way public business is conducted gives a fairly clear sign of the actual state of morals and the health of the body politic. The more harmony reigns in the assemblies, that is, the closer opinion comes to unanimity, the stronger the general will is. Long debates, dissension and tumult, on the other hand, announce the rise of particular interests and the decline of the State.

This seems less clear when the constitution includes two or more orders, as the patricians and plebeians did at Rome. Quarrels between those two orders often disturbed the comitia, even in the best days of the Republic. But the exception is more apparent than real. Because of a defect built into that body politic, there were, so to speak, two States in one, and what is not true of the two together is true of each separately. Indeed, even in the stormiest times, the plebiscita of the people, when the Senate did not interfere, always passed quietly and by large majorities. Since the citizens had but one interest, the people had but a single will.

At the opposite end of the circle, unanimity returns. This happens when citizens have fallen into servitude and have lost both liberty and will. Then fear and flattery turn votes into acclamation. Deliberation ends, and only worship or cursing is left. That was the vile way the senate expressed its views under the Emperors, sometimes with absurd precautions. Tacitus observes that under Otho the senators, while heaping curses on Vitellius, contrived at the same time to make a deafening noise, so that if he ever became their master, he would not know what each of them had said.

The rules for counting votes and comparing opinions depend on these various considerations. They should be adjusted according to how easy or hard the general will is to discover, and how far the State has declined.

Only one law, by its nature, requires unanimous consent: the social compact. Civil association is the most voluntary of all acts. Since every man is born free and his own master, no one, under any pretext whatever, can make him a subject without his consent. To decide that the son of a slave is born a slave is to decide that he is not born a man.

Suppose, then, that some people oppose the social compact when it is made. Their opposition does not invalidate the contract; it only leaves them outside it. They are foreigners among citizens. Once the State exists, living in its territory amounts to consent, because to dwell there is to submit to the Sovereign.[1]

Except for this original contract, the majority vote always binds everyone else, and this follows from the contract itself. But people ask how a man can be free and still be forced to conform to wills that are not his own. How can the opponents be free and yet subject to laws they never agreed to?

I answer that the question is badly put. The citizen consents to all the laws, including those passed over his opposition, and even those that punish him when he dares to break one. The constant will of all the members of the State is the general will, and through it they are citizens and free.[2] When a law is proposed in the popular assembly, the people is not being asked exactly whether it approves or rejects the proposal, but whether the proposal conforms to the general will, which is their will. Each man, in casting his vote, states his opinion on that point, and the general will is found by counting the votes. So when the opinion contrary to mine prevails, this proves only that I was mistaken, and that what I took to be the general will was not. Had my particular opinion won, I would have achieved the opposite of what I willed, and in that case I would not have been free.
This assumes, of course, that all the qualities of the general will still lie in the majority. When they no longer do, then whichever side a man takes, liberty is no longer possible.

In showing earlier how particular wills take the place of the general will in public deliberation, I pointed out adequately the practical ways of avoiding this abuse, and I will say more about them later. I have also given the principles for fixing the proportion of votes needed to declare that will. One vote of difference destroys equality, and a single opponent destroys unanimity. Between equality and unanimity, though, there are several grades of unequal division, and the proportion can be set at any of them according to the condition and needs of the body politic.

Two general rules can serve to regulate this proportion. First, the graver and more important the questions under discussion, the closer the prevailing opinion should come to unanimity. Second, the more urgent the matter, the smaller the required margin of votes may be allowed to become: when a decision must be made on the spot, a majority of one should suffice. The first rule seems more in harmony with the laws, and the second with practical affairs. In any case, the two together give the best proportions for deciding the majority needed.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 3 — Elections
paragraphs: The elections of the prince and the magistrates are, as I have said, complex acts, and there are two possible ways to carry them out: choice and lot. Various republics have used both, and a highly complicated mixture of the two still survives in the election of the Doge of Venice.

“Election by lot,” says Montesquieu, “is democratic by nature.” I agree that it is, but in what sense? “The lot,” he goes on, “is a way of choosing that is unfair to no one; it leaves each citizen a reasonable hope of serving his country.” These are not reasons.

Remember that electing rulers is a function of government, not of Sovereignty. Then we will see why the lot is the method more natural to democracy, where the fewer acts the administration performs, the better it is.

In every real democracy, holding office is not an advantage but a burdensome charge, which cannot fairly be laid on one person rather than another. Only the law can impose the charge on whoever the lot falls on. For then the conditions are the same for everyone, and the choice depends on no human will, so no particular application alters the universality of the law.
In an aristocracy the prince chooses the prince, so the government preserves itself, and voting is set up as it should be.

The example of the Doge of Venice’s election confirms this distinction instead of undermining it: a mixed form suits a mixed government. It is a mistake to take the government of Venice for a real aristocracy. If the people has no share in the government, the nobility is itself the people. A host of poor Barnabotes never get near any magistracy, and their nobility amounts to the empty title of Excellency and the right to sit in the Great Council. This Great Council is as large as our General Council at Geneva, and its illustrious members have no more privileges than our ordinary citizens. It cannot be disputed that, setting aside the enormous difference between the two republics, the _bourgeoisie_ of Geneva corresponds exactly to the _patriciate_ of Venice; our _natives_ and _inhabitants_ correspond to the _townsmen_ and the _people_ of Venice; and our _peasants_ correspond to the _subjects_ on the mainland. However one looks at that republic, leaving its size out of account, its government is no more aristocratic than our own. The only difference is that, since we have no ruler for life, we do not need to use the lot as Venice does.

In a real democracy, election by lot would have few drawbacks. Equality would exist everywhere, in morals and talents as well as in principles and fortunes, so it would hardly matter who was chosen. But as I have already said, a real democracy is only an ideal.

When choice and lot are used together, choice should fill the positions that need special talents, such as military posts. Lot does for cases like judicial offices, where good sense, justice and integrity are enough, since in a well-constituted State all the citizens share these qualities.

Monarchical government has no place for lot or vote. The monarch is by right the only prince and only magistrate, so the choice of his lieutenants belongs to him alone. When the Abbé de Saint-Pierre proposed multiplying the Councils of the King of France and electing their members by ballot, he did not see that he was proposing to change the form of government.

Next I should discuss how opinions are given and counted in the assembly of the people. But an account of this part of the Roman constitution may illustrate all the rules I could lay down more forcefully. A thoughtful reader will find it worth following in some detail how public and private affairs were run in a Council of two hundred thousand men.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 4 — The Roman Comitia
paragraphs: We have no well-documented records of Rome’s earliest period. Most of the stories told about it are very probably fables. In general, the most instructive part of any people’s history, the part about how it was founded, is the part we know least about. Experience shows us every day what causes lead to the revolutions of empires. But since no new peoples are formed now, we have almost nothing but guesswork to explain how they were created.

Whatever customs we find in place must have had some origin, at least. The traditions that go back to those origins, that carry the greatest authority and that the strongest proofs confirm should count as the most certain. These are the rules I have tried to follow while asking how the freest and most powerful people on earth used its supreme power.

After Rome was founded, the new-born republic, meaning the army of its founder, made up of Albans, Sabines and foreigners, was divided into three groups. From this division they took the name _tribes_. Each tribe was split into ten _curiæ_, and each _curia_ into _decuriæ_, led by officers called _curiones_ and _decuriones_.

In addition, each tribe supplied a body of one hundred _Equites_, or Knights, called a _century_. This shows that these divisions, which a town had no need of, were at first purely military. Yet an instinct for greatness seems to have led the little town of Rome to give itself, in advance, a political system fit for the capital of the world.

This original division soon produced an awkward situation. The tribes of the Albans (Ramnenses) and the Sabines (Tatienses) always stayed the same size, while the tribe of the foreigners (Luceres) kept growing as more and more foreigners came to live in Rome, so that it soon outstripped the others in strength. Servius fixed this dangerous flaw by changing the basis of the division. He abolished the division by race and put in its place a new one, based on the quarter of the town each tribe lived in. Instead of three tribes he created four, each occupying one of the hills of Rome and named after it. In this way he corrected the inequality of the moment and also provided for the future. And so that the division would be one of persons as well as of places, he forbade the inhabitants of one quarter to move to another, which prevented the races from mixing.

He also doubled the three old centuries of Knights and added twelve more, keeping the old names. With this simple and prudent method he marked off the Knights from the people, and the people did not complain.

To the four urban tribes Servius added fifteen more, called rural tribes because they were made up of people living in the country, which was divided into fifteen cantons. Fifteen more were created later, and the Roman people ended up in thirty-five tribes, which is how it stayed until the end of the Republic.

The split between urban and rural tribes had one effect worth noting, both because nothing like it is found elsewhere and because Rome owed to it the preservation of her morals and the growth of her empire. We would expect the urban tribes to take over power and honors quickly and to start running down the rural tribes. What happened was exactly the opposite. The taste of the early Romans for country life is well known. They owed it to their wise founder, who tied farming and military service to liberty and, so to speak, banished arts, crafts, intrigue, fortune and slavery to the town.

Since all of Rome’s most illustrious citizens lived on the land and farmed it, people grew used to looking there, and nowhere else, for the mainstays of the republic. This was the way of life of the best patricians, so everyone honored it. The simple, hard-working life of the villager was preferred to the lazy, idle life of the _bourgeoisie_ of Rome. A man who would have been a wretched proletarian in town became a respected citizen as a farm laborer. Varro says, not without reason, that our great-souled ancestors set up the nursery of sturdy, brave men in the village: men who defended them in war and fed them in peace. Pliny states flatly that the country tribes were honored because of the men who made them up, while cowards whom people wanted to disgrace were moved to the town tribes as a public shame. The Sabine Appius Claudius, when he came to settle in Rome, was loaded with honors and enrolled in a rural tribe, which later took his family name. Finally, freedmen always entered the urban tribes and never the rural ones. Nor is there a single example in the whole Republic of a freedman, even once he had become a citizen, reaching any magistracy.
This was an excellent rule. But it was carried so far that it eventually brought a change in the political system, and certainly an abuse.

First, the censors had long claimed the right to transfer citizens arbitrarily from one tribe to another. They then allowed most people to enroll themselves in whatever tribe they liked. This permission certainly did no good, and it also took away one of the censorship’s greatest resources. Moreover, the great and powerful all had themselves enrolled in the country tribes, while the freedmen who had become citizens stayed with the common people in the town tribes. As a result, both kinds of tribe soon lost any local or territorial meaning. They became so mixed up that the members of one could not be told from those of another except by the registers. The idea of the word _tribe_ thus became personal instead of real, or rather came to be little more than a fantasy.
On top of this, the town tribes, being on the spot, were often the stronger in the comitia, and they sold the State to anyone who would stoop to buy the votes of the rabble that made them up.

The founder had set up ten _curiæ_ in each tribe, so the whole Roman people, which was then contained within the city walls, consisted of thirty _curiæ_. Each had its own temples, gods, officers, priests and festivals. The festivals were called _compitalia_ and matched the _paganalia_ that the rural tribes held in later times.

When Servius made his new division, the thirty _curiæ_ could not be shared equally among his four tribes, and he did not want to disturb them. So they became another way of dividing the inhabitants of Rome, entirely independent of the tribes. But the rural tribes and their members had nothing to do with _curiæ_: by then the tribes had become a purely civil institution, and since a new way of raising troops had been introduced, the military divisions of Romulus were no longer needed. So although every citizen was enrolled in a tribe, there were very many who did not belong to a _curia_.

Servius made a third division as well, entirely separate from the other two, and in its effects it proved the most important of all. He sorted the whole Roman people into six classes, set apart not by place or by person but by wealth. The rich went into the first classes, the poor into the last, and people of moderate means into those between. These six classes were divided again into one hundred and ninety-three bodies called centuries, arranged so that the first class alone had more than half of them and the last had just one. The class with the fewest members therefore had the most centuries, and the whole last class counted as one subdivision, even though it alone contained more than half the inhabitants of Rome.

To keep the people from seeing too clearly what this arrangement would lead to, Servius tried to give it a military look. In the second class he placed two centuries of armorers, and in the fourth two of makers of weapons. In every class except the last he separated young and old, that is, those obliged to bear arms from those whose age legally exempted them. This distinction, more than that of wealth, made it necessary to repeat the census, or counting, often. Finally, he ordered the assembly to be held in the Campus Martius, and everyone of an age to serve to come there armed.

He did not make this division of young and old in the last class as well because the common people who composed it were not granted the right to bear arms for their country. A man had to own a hearth to acquire the right to defend it. Of all the troops of beggars who today lend luster to the armies of kings, there is perhaps not one who would not have been driven with scorn out of a Roman cohort, in the days when soldiers were the defenders of liberty.

Within this last class, though, _proletarians_ were set apart from _capite censi._ The proletarians were not quite reduced to nothing: they at least gave the State citizens, and at times of pressing need even soldiers. Those who had nothing at all, and could be counted only by heads, were considered worth nothing whatever. Marius was the first to stoop to enlisting them.

I will not now decide whether this third arrangement was good or bad in itself. But I think I can say that it could work only because the early Romans had simple morals, no self-interest, a love of farming, and a scorn for trade and for the love of gain. Where is the modern people among whom devouring greed, restlessness, intrigue, constant moves and endless swings of fortune would let such a system last twenty years without turning the State upside down? We must also note that at Rome morality and the censorship, which were stronger than this institution, corrected its faults, and that a rich man found himself demoted to the class of the poor for making too much display of his wealth.

All this makes it easy to see why people almost always mention only five classes, even though there were really six. The sixth supplied no soldiers to the army and no votes in the Campus Martius,[1] and it had almost no function in the State, so it was rarely thought to matter.

These, then, were the ways the Roman people was divided. Now let us look at how this affected the assemblies. A lawfully summoned assembly was called a _comitia_. Comitia usually met in the public square at Rome or in the Campus Martius, and they went by the names _Comitia Curiata, Comitia Centuriata_, and _Comitia Tributa_, depending on the form in which they were called together. Romulus founded the _Comitia Curiata_, Servius the _Centuriata_, and the tribunes of the people the _Tributa_. No law was approved and no magistrate elected anywhere but in the comitia. Every citizen was enrolled in a _curia_, a century or a tribe, so no citizen was shut out of the vote, and the Roman people was truly sovereign both _de jure_ and _de facto_.

Three conditions had to be met before the comitia could lawfully assemble and their acts have the force of law. First, the body or magistrate calling them needed the proper authority. Second, the meeting had to fall on a day the law allowed. Third, the auguries had to be favorable.

The reason for the first rule needs no explaining. The second is a matter of policy. For example, the comitia could not be held on festivals or market days, when country people came to Rome on business and had no time to spend the day in the public square. Through the third, the senate held the proud, restless people in check and properly restrained the ardor of seditious tribunes, who nonetheless found more than one way around this obstacle.

The comitia did not only vote on laws and elect rulers. The Roman people had taken the most important functions of government into its own hands, so one can say that the fate of Europe was settled in its assemblies. Because their business varied so much, the assemblies took different forms, depending on what they had to decide.

To judge these various forms, it is enough to compare them. When Romulus set up the _curiæ_, he meant the people to check the senate and the senate to check the people, while he kept his own ascendancy over both. So through this assembly he gave the people all the authority of numbers, to balance the power and riches he left to the patricians. But in keeping with the spirit of monarchy, he still left the patricians a greater advantage, in the influence their clients had on the majority of votes. This excellent institution of patron and client was a masterpiece of statesmanship and humanity. Without it the patriciate, which flatly contradicted the republican spirit, could not have survived. Rome alone has the honor of having given the world this great example, which never led to any abuse and yet has never been followed.
Under the kings the assemblies by _curiæ_ continued until Servius, and since the reign of the later Tarquin was not regarded as legitimate, royal laws were commonly called _leges curiatæ_.

Under the Republic the _curiæ_ stayed limited to the four urban tribes and held only the populace of Rome. They pleased neither the senate, which led the patricians, nor the tribunes, who, plebeians though they were, led the well-to-do citizens. They therefore lost standing, and fell so low that thirty lictors would meet and do the work the _Comitia Curiata_ ought to have done.

The division by centuries favored the aristocracy so strongly that at first it is hard to see how the senate could ever have lost in the comitia named after them, the ones that elected the consuls, the censors and the other curule magistrates. The six classes of the whole Roman people were divided into a hundred and ninety-three centuries, and the first class held ninety-eight of them. Votes were counted by centuries alone, so this class by itself outvoted all the rest. When all its centuries agreed, the other votes were not even taken: the choice of the smallest number stood as the choice of the multitude. One may say that in the _Comitia Centuriata_ decisions were governed far more by the depth of purses than by the number of votes.

Two things, however, tempered this extreme power. First, the tribunes, as a rule, and a great many plebeians always belonged to the class of the rich, and they offset the influence of the patricians in the first class.

The second way was this. The centuries were not made to vote straight through in order, which would always have meant starting with the first. Instead the Romans always picked one by lot, and it voted alone. Then on another day all the centuries were summoned in order of rank, the same election was repeated, and as a rule confirmed. In this way the authority of example was taken away from rank and given to the lot, on a democratic principle.

This custom had a further advantage. Between the two elections, citizens from the country had time to learn about the merits of the candidate provisionally chosen, so they did not have to vote without knowing the case. But under the pretext of speeding things up, the custom was abolished, and both elections were held on the same day.

The _Comitia Tributa_ were really the council of the Roman people. Only the tribunes could call them together. The tribunes were elected there, and their plebiscita passed there. The senate had no standing in them and not even the right to attend. Senators were forced to obey laws they could not vote on, so in this respect they were less free than the humblest citizens. This injustice was thoroughly ill-conceived, and it was enough by itself to invalidate the decrees of a body that did not admit all its members. Suppose all the patricians had attended the comitia by right as citizens. As mere private individuals they would not have had much influence on a vote counted by heads, where the humblest proletarian counted as much as the _princeps senatus_.

So we can see that, besides the order gained by these various ways of distributing so large a people and collecting its votes, the methods were not forms that made no difference in themselves. The results of each depended on the aims for which it was preferred.

Without going into more detail, we can gather from the above that the _Comitia Tributa_ best suited popular government, and the _Comitia Centuriata_ aristocracy. In the _Comitia Curiata_ the populace of Rome was the majority, and it was fit only to advance tyranny and evil designs. Naturally it fell into disrepute, and even seditious people stayed away from a method that exposed their plans too openly. There is no disputing that the whole majesty of the Roman people lay in the _Comitia Centuriata_ alone, because it alone included everyone. The _Comitia Curiata_ left out the rural tribes, and the _Comitia Tributa_ left out the senate and the patricians.

The way of taking the vote was as simple among the ancient Romans as their morals, though not as simple as at Sparta. Each man called out his vote, and a clerk wrote it down. The majority in each tribe determined the tribe’s vote, the majority of the tribes determined the people’s, and the same went for _curiæ_ and centuries. This custom worked well while honesty won out among the citizens and each man was ashamed to vote openly for an unjust proposal or an unworthy candidate. But once the people grew corrupt and votes were bought, it became fitting for voting to be secret, so that buyers would be held back by mistrust and rogues given a way of not being traitors.

I know that Cicero attacks this change and blames it in part for the ruin of the Republic. I feel the weight Cicero’s authority must carry on such a point, but I cannot agree with him. I hold, on the contrary, that too few changes like this will hasten the destruction of the State. A diet that keeps the healthy well does not suit the sick, and in the same way we should not try to govern a corrupted people with the laws a good people requires. There is no better proof of this rule than the long life of the Republic of Venice, whose shadow still exists, solely because its laws suit only wicked men.

So the citizens were given tablets, which let each man vote without anyone knowing how he voted. New methods were also introduced for collecting the tablets, counting the voices, comparing the numbers, and so on. Yet all these precautions did not stop the good faith of the officers in charge of these tasks[2] from often being suspect. Finally, edicts were issued to prevent intrigues and trafficking in votes, but their very number shows how useless they were.

Toward the close of the Republic, extraordinary expedients were often needed to make up for the inadequacy of the laws. Sometimes miracles were supposed. This could fool the people but not those who governed. Sometimes an assembly was called in a hurry, before the candidates had time to form their factions. Sometimes a whole sitting was filled with talk, when it was seen that the people had been won over and was about to take the wrong side. But in the end ambition got around every attempt to check it. And the most incredible fact of all is that, in the midst of all these abuses, the vast people, thanks to its ancient regulations, never stopped electing magistrates, passing laws, judging cases and carrying on public and private business, almost as easily as the senate itself could have done.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 5 — The Tribunate
paragraphs: Sometimes the parts that make up the State cannot be held in exact proportion, or causes that cannot be removed keep shifting how one part stands toward another. The remedy then is a special magistracy that does not merge into the body of the State. It puts each term back in its right relation to the others, and it serves as a link, a middle term, between prince and people, or between prince and Sovereign, or, where necessary, between both at once.

This body I shall call the _tribunate_. It guards the laws and the legislative power. At times it shields the Sovereign from the government, as the tribunes of the people did at Rome. At times it backs the government against the people, as the Council of Ten does today at Venice. And at times it keeps the two in balance, as the Ephors did at Sparta.

The tribunate is not a constituent part of the city, and it should hold no share of legislative or executive power. Yet that is exactly what makes its power greater: it can do nothing, but it can stop anything from being done. As defender of the laws it is more sacred and more revered than the prince who carries them out or the Sovereign who enacts them. Rome showed this plainly, when the proud patricians, who despised the people, had to bow before one of its officers, a man with neither auspices nor jurisdiction.

A tribunate that is wisely tempered is the firmest support a good constitution can have. But if its strength goes even slightly too far, it throws the whole State into disorder. Weakness, by contrast, is not in its nature: so long as it is anything at all, it is never less than it ought to be.

It slides into tyranny when it seizes the executive power, which it ought only to restrain, and when it tries to do without the laws, which it ought only to protect. The immense power of the Ephors did no harm while Sparta kept its morals, but once corruption had set in, that power sped it along. Agis was slaughtered by these tyrants, and his successor Cleomenes avenged his blood. The Ephors’ crime and their punishment both hastened the ruin of the republic, and after Cleomenes Sparta counted for nothing. Rome fell the same way. The tribunes grabbed more and more power, bit by bit, and in the end that power, together with laws made to secure liberty, shielded the emperors who destroyed it. As for the Venetian Council of Ten, it is a tribunal of blood, dreaded by patricians and people alike. It no longer offers the laws any lofty protection, now that they have been degraded. It simply strikes in the dark, and no one dares to take note of the blows.

Like the government, the tribunate grows weaker as the number of its members increases. The tribunes of the Roman people, who at first numbered only two and then five, wished to double that number. The senate let them, confident that it could use one tribune to check another, as indeed it later did freely.

The best way to prevent usurpations by so formidable a body would be not to make it permanent, but to regulate the periods during which it stays in abeyance, though no government has yet used this method. These intervals should not be long enough to give abuses time to grow strong. They may be fixed by law in such a way that they can easily be shortened, when necessary, by extraordinary commissions.

I see no drawback in this method. As I have said, the tribunate is no part of the constitution, so removing it leaves the constitution untouched. The method also seems effective, because a magistrate who has just been restored begins with the power the law gives him, not the power his predecessor wielded.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 6 — The Dictatorship
paragraphs: The laws are inflexible and cannot adapt themselves to circumstances. In certain cases this may make them disastrous, and at a time of crisis cause the ruin of the State. The order and slowness of the forms they prescribe require a stretch of time that circumstances sometimes refuse. A thousand cases may arise for which the legislator has made no provision, and part of being foresighted, and a very necessary part, is to know that everything cannot be foreseen.
It is wrong, therefore, to want political institutions so strong that it becomes impossible to suspend their operation. Even Sparta let its laws lapse.

Still, only the gravest dangers can outweigh the danger of altering the public order, and the sacred authority of the laws should be halted only when the existence of the country itself is at stake. In these rare and obvious cases, a special act provides for the public safety by placing it in the hands of the worthiest man. How this is done depends on the kind of danger.

Sometimes the remedy is simply a more active government. Then power is gathered in the hands of one or two of its members, and what changes is not the authority of the laws but only the way they are administered. But sometimes the peril is such that the machinery of the laws stands in the way of saving the State. Then the answer is to appoint a supreme ruler, who silences all the laws and for a moment suspends the sovereign authority. In such a case no one can doubt what the general will is, and it is clear that the people’s first intention is that the State should not perish. So suspending the legislative authority is in no sense abolishing it. The magistrate who silences it cannot make it speak. He dominates it, but he cannot represent it. He can do anything except make laws.

The Roman senate took the first course when it used a consecrated formula to charge the consuls with seeing to the safety of the Republic. The second course was taken when one of the two consuls appointed a dictator,[1] a custom Rome had borrowed from Alba.

In the early years of the Republic, Rome turned to the dictatorship very often. The State was not yet on a footing firm enough to stand by the strength of its constitution alone. The morals of the time made many precautions needless that would have been necessary in other periods. Nobody feared that a dictator would abuse his authority or try to hold it past his term. Quite the opposite: so much power seemed a burden to the man who wore it, and he hurried to lay it down, as if standing in for the laws were too troublesome and too dangerous a post to hold on to.

So what makes me criticize the careless use of this supreme magistracy in the earliest times is not the danger that it would be abused but the danger that it would be cheapened. It was used freely for elections, dedications and mere formalities. That risked making it less fearsome when it was truly needed, and teaching men to treat as empty a title they had only ever seen used at empty ceremonies.

Near the end of the Republic, the Romans had grown more wary, and they were as unreasonably stingy with the dictatorship as they had once been generous. It is easy to see that their fears had no foundation. The capital was too weak to be a threat, and that protected it from the magistrates in its midst. A dictator might in some cases defend public liberty, but he could never endanger it. And the chains of Rome would be forged not in Rome itself but in her armies. How feebly Marius resisted Sulla, and Pompey resisted Caesar, showed clearly what authority at home could expect to achieve against force from abroad.

This mistake led the Romans into serious blunders. One example is their failure to appoint a dictator during the Catilinarian conspiracy. Only the city itself was involved, plus at most a province of Italy, and the unlimited authority the laws gave a dictator would have let him dispose of the conspiracy quickly. As it was, the plot was crushed only through a run of lucky accidents that human prudence had no right to count on.

Instead the senate settled for handing all its power to the consuls. To act effectively, Cicero therefore had to go beyond his powers on a matter of life and death. In the first rush of joy his conduct was approved, but later he was rightly made to answer for the blood of citizens spilled against the laws. No one could ever have said that of a dictator. But the consul’s eloquence won the day. Roman though he was, he loved his own glory more than his country, and he looked less for the most lawful and secure way of saving the State than for a way to claim all the honor of saving it himself.[2] So he was rightly honored as the liberator of Rome, and rightly punished as a lawbreaker. However brilliant his recall may have been, it was undoubtedly an act of pardon.

However this weighty trust is conferred, its term should be set very short and made impossible to extend. The crises that call for it end quickly, either in the State’s ruin or in its rescue. Once the immediate need is past, the dictatorship turns into either tyranny or a dead letter. At Rome dictators held office for six months only, and most of them resigned before the time was up. With a longer term, they might well have tried to stretch it further, as the decemvirs did when they were elected for a year. A dictator had time only to meet the need for which he was chosen, and none to think up other projects.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 7 — The Censorship
paragraphs: The law declares the general will, and in the same way the censorship declares the public judgment. Public opinion is the kind of law that the censor administers, and like the prince, he applies it only to particular cases.
The censorial tribunal does not rule on the people’s opinion. It only declares it, and as soon as the two part ways, its decisions are null and void.

It is useless to distinguish the morals of a nation from the things it esteems; both depend on the same principle and cannot be told apart. There is no people on earth whose choice of pleasures is decided by nature rather than opinion. Set men’s opinions right, and their morals will purify themselves. Men always love what is good, or what they find good; it is in judging what is good that they go wrong. So it is this judgment that must be regulated. Whoever judges of morals judges of honor, and whoever judges of honor finds his law in opinion.

A people’s opinions spring from its constitution. The law does not regulate morals, but it is legislation that gives birth to them. When legislation weakens, morals decay. In that situation, though, the censors’ judgment will not achieve what the force of the laws could not.

It follows that the censorship may be useful for preserving morals, but can never be useful for restoring them. Set up censors while the laws are vigorous; once the laws have lost their vigor, all hope is gone, for no legitimate power can keep its force when the laws have lost theirs.

The censorship preserves morals by keeping opinion from growing corrupt, by keeping it sound through wise applications, and sometimes even by settling it while it is still undecided. In the kingdom of France, the use of seconds in duels had gone to wild extremes. A few words in a royal edict ended it: “As for those who are cowards enough to call upon seconds.” This judgment got ahead of the public’s own and settled the matter at once. But when edicts from the same source tried to declare dueling itself an act of cowardice, which it is, the public paid no attention. Common opinion does not see it that way, and on this point the public’s mind was already made up.

I have said elsewhere[1] that public opinion is not subject to any constraint, so the tribunal set up to represent it should show no trace of constraint. One cannot admire too much the skill with which the Romans, and even more the Lacedaemonians, used this resource, which we moderns have lost entirely.

In the Spartan Council, a man of bad morals once made a good proposal. The Ephors set it aside and had a virtuous citizen put forward the same one. What an honor for the one man, and what a disgrace for the other, with neither praised nor blamed! Some drunkards from Samos[2] fouled the tribunal of the Ephors. The next day a public edict allowed Samians to be filthy. No actual punishment could have stung as much as that impunity. When Sparta has ruled on what is right and what is not, Greece does not appeal.
