chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 8 — Civil Religion
paragraphs: In the beginning, men had no kings except the gods, and no government except theocracy. They reasoned like Caligula, and at that time they reasoned correctly. Feelings take a long time to change before men can bring themselves to accept their equals as masters, in the hope of gaining something by it.

Since God stood over every political society, there were as many gods as there were peoples. Two peoples who were strangers to each other, and nearly always enemies, could not long accept the same master, just as two armies in battle cannot follow the same commander. Division into nations therefore produced polytheism, and polytheism in turn produced theological and civil intolerance, which, as we shall see later, are by nature the same thing.

The Greeks liked to rediscover their own gods among the barbarians. That came from seeing themselves as the natural Sovereigns of those peoples. But nothing is more absurd than the scholarship of our own day, which identifies and mixes up the gods of different nations. As if Moloch, Saturn and Chronos could be the same god! As if the Phoenician Baal, the Greek Zeus and the Latin Jupiter could be the same! As if imaginary beings with different names could still have anything in common!

If you ask how pagan times, when every State had its own cult and its own gods, managed to avoid wars of religion, my answer is that this was exactly the reason. Each State had its own cult as well as its own government, so it drew no line between its gods and its laws. Political war was also theological war, and the territories of the gods were, so to speak, set by the borders of nations. The god of one people had no rights over another. The gods of the pagans were not jealous gods; they shared the empire of the world among themselves. Even Moses and the Hebrews sometimes went along with this view when they spoke of the God of Israel. It is true that they considered the gods of the Canaanites powerless, since the Canaanites were a condemned people marked for destruction, whose land the Hebrews were to take. But remember how they spoke of the neighboring peoples they were forbidden to attack! “Is not what belongs to your god Chamos yours by right?” said Jephthah to the Ammonites. “We hold the same title to the lands our conquering God has made his own.”[1] Here, I think, is an acknowledgment that the rights of Chamos and those of the God of Israel are of the same kind.

But the Jews came under the kings of Babylon and later those of Syria, and they stubbornly refused to recognize any god but their own. Their conquerors took this refusal as rebellion, and it brought on them the persecutions we read about in their history, which have no parallel until the coming of Christianity.[2]

Every religion was tied only to the laws of the State that prescribed it. So there was no way to convert a people except by enslaving it, and the only missionaries could be conquerors. Changing cults was the law that the defeated had to accept, so one had to win a victory before proposing such a change. Far from men fighting for the gods, the gods fought for men, as in Homer: each side asked its god for victory and repaid him with new altars. Before taking a city, the Romans called on its gods to leave it. When they left the Tarentines their outraged gods, they treated those gods as subordinate to their own and forced to pay them homage. They left the defeated their gods just as they left them their laws. A wreath for the Jupiter of the Capitol was often the only tribute they demanded.

In the end, the Romans spread their cult and their gods along with their empire, and they often adopted those of the peoples they had defeated, granting the rights of the city to both alike. So the peoples of that vast empire gradually found themselves with multitudes of gods and cults, almost the same everywhere. In this way paganism throughout the known world at last became one and the same religion.

This was the situation when Jesus came to set up a spiritual kingdom on earth. By separating the theological system from the political one, he made the State cease to be one, and he caused the internal divisions that have never stopped troubling Christian peoples. The idea of a kingdom of the other world could never have occurred to pagans, so they always saw the Christians as real rebels: people who pretended to submit while waiting for the chance to make themselves independent, become the masters, and cunningly seize the authority they pretended, in their weakness, to respect. That was the cause of the persecutions.

The pagans’ fear came true. Everything then changed. The humble Christians altered their tone, and before long this so-called kingdom of the other world, under a visible head, became the most violent despotism on earth.

Yet there has always been a prince and there have always been civil laws. This double power and clash of jurisdictions has made good government impossible in Christian States, and people have never managed to work out whether they owed obedience to the master or to the priest.

Several peoples, even in Europe and nearby, have tried without success to keep or restore the old system, but the spirit of Christianity has prevailed everywhere. The sacred cult has always stayed independent of the Sovereign, or become so again, with no necessary link to the body of the State. Mahomet held very sound views and tied his political system together well. As long as his form of government lasted under the caliphs who succeeded him, it was truly one government, and to that extent good. But the Arabs grew prosperous, lettered, civilized, slack and cowardly, and barbarians conquered them. The division between the two powers began again. It is less visible among Mahometans than among Christians, but it exists all the same, especially in the sect of Ali, and in some States, such as Persia, it is felt constantly.

In our own world, the Kings of England have made themselves heads of the Church, and so have the Czars. Yet the title has turned them into ministers of the Church more than its masters. What they have gained is the power to keep the Church going, not the right to change it; they are not its legislators, only its princes. Wherever the clergy forms a corporate body,[3] it is the master and legislator in its own country. So England and Russia, like other countries, have two powers and two Sovereigns.

Of all Christian writers, only the philosopher Hobbes saw the evil and its remedy. He dared to propose reuniting the two heads of the eagle and restoring political unity everywhere, without which no State or government will ever be properly constituted. But he should have seen that the domineering spirit of Christianity cannot be reconciled with his system, and that the interest of the priests would always be stronger than that of the State. What has drawn hatred on his political theory is not so much what is false and terrible in it as what is just and true.[4]

I believe that if history were studied from this angle, it would be easy to refute Bayle and Warburton, who hold opposite opinions. Bayle says religion can be of no use to the body politic; Warburton, on the contrary, says Christianity is its strongest support. We could show Bayle that no State has ever been founded without a religious basis, and Warburton that Christian law at bottom does more harm by weakening the State’s constitution than good by strengthening it. To make myself understood, I only have to sharpen the too vague ideas about religion that bear on this subject.

Religion, when considered in relation to society (which is either general or particular), can also be divided into two kinds: the religion of man and the religion of the citizen. The first has no temples, altars or rites. It is limited to the purely inward worship of the supreme God and the eternal duties of morality. It is the religion of the Gospel, pure and simple, true theism, what we may call natural divine right or law. The other kind is established in a single country and gives that country its gods, its own guardian patrons. It has its dogmas, its rites, and an outward worship prescribed by law. Outside the one nation that follows it, the whole world is in its eyes unbelieving, foreign and barbarous; it extends the duties and rights of man only as far as its own altars. All the religions of early peoples were of this kind, and we may define it as civil or positive divine right or law.

A third kind of religion is stranger still. It gives men two codes of law, two rulers and two countries, subjects them to contradictory duties, and makes it impossible for them to be faithful both to religion and to citizenship. The religions of the Lamas and of the Japanese are of this sort, and so is Roman Christianity, which may be called the religion of the priest. The result is a mixed, anti-social code that has no name.

Viewed politically, all three kinds of religion have their defects. The third is so plainly bad that it is a waste of time to stop and prove it. Everything that destroys social unity is worthless; every institution that sets a man in contradiction with himself is worthless.

The second kind is good because it joins the worship of the gods to love of the laws. It makes the country the object of the citizens’ devotion and teaches them that serving the State is serving its guardian god. It is a form of theocracy, in which there can be no pontiff but the prince and no priests but the magistrates. To die for one’s country then becomes martyrdom; to break its laws is impiety; and to expose a guilty man to public curses is to hand him over to the anger of the gods: _Sacer estod_.

On the other hand, this religion is bad because it is founded on lies and error. It deceives men, makes them credulous and superstitious, and smothers the true worship of the Divinity under empty ritual. It is bad again when it becomes tyrannical and exclusive and turns a people bloodthirsty and intolerant, so that the people breathe fire and slaughter and consider it a sacred act to kill anyone who does not believe in their gods. This puts such a people in a natural state of war with all others, which gravely endangers its own security.

What remains, then, is the religion of man, or Christianity. I do not mean the Christianity of today but that of the Gospel, which is entirely different. Through this holy, sublime and true religion, all men are children of one God and recognize one another as brothers, and the society that unites them is not dissolved even by death.

But this religion has no particular connection with the body politic. It leaves the laws with the force they have in themselves, without adding anything to it, so one of the great bonds that hold each separate society together fails to work. What is more, far from binding the hearts of the citizens to the State, it draws them away from all earthly things. I know nothing more contrary to the social spirit.

People tell us that a nation of true Christians would form the most perfect society imaginable. I see only one serious problem with this idea: a society of true Christians would not be a society of human beings.

I will go further: such a society, perfect as it is, would be neither the strongest nor the most lasting. Its very perfection would strip it of its bond of union, and the flaw that destroyed it would lie in that perfection itself.

Everyone would do his duty. The people would obey the laws, the rulers would be just and moderate, the magistrates upright and incorruptible, and the soldiers would despise death. There would be no vanity and no luxury. So far, so good, but let us hear the rest.

Christianity as a religion is wholly spiritual and concerned only with heavenly things; the Christian’s country is not of this world. He does his duty, but with deep indifference to whether his efforts succeed or fail. As long as he has nothing to reproach himself with, it matters little to him whether things go well or badly here on earth. If the State prospers, he hardly dares take part in the public happiness, for fear of growing proud of his country’s glory. If the State is wasting away, he blesses the hand of God that lies heavy on His people.

For the State to be peaceful and harmony to be kept, every citizen without exception would have to be a good Christian. If bad luck produced a single self-seeker or hypocrite, a Catiline or a Cromwell for instance, he would certainly get the better of his pious fellow citizens. Christian charity does not readily let a man think badly of his neighbors. Once he has found some trick for deceiving them and getting a share of public authority, you have a man established in dignity, and it is God’s will that he be respected. Very soon you have a power, and it is God’s will that it be obeyed. If the man who holds that power abuses it, it is the scourge with which God punishes His children. There would be scruples about driving out the usurper: public tranquility would have to be disturbed, violence used and blood spilled, and all this fits badly with Christian meekness. And after all, in this vale of sorrows, what does it matter whether we are free men or serfs? The essential thing is to get to heaven, and resignation is one more way of getting there.

If war breaks out with another State, the citizens march willingly to battle. None of them thinks of running away; they do their duty, but with no passion for victory. They know better how to die than how to win. What does it matter to them whether they win or lose? Does Providence not know better than they do what is good for them? Just think how a proud, impetuous and passionate enemy could turn their stoicism to account! Set against them those generous peoples who were devoured by a fierce love of glory and of their country. Picture your Christian republic facing Sparta or Rome. The pious Christians will be beaten, crushed and destroyed before they know what has happened, or will be saved only because their enemy comes to despise them. I think the oath of Fabius’s soldiers was a fine one: they swore not to conquer or die, but to return victorious, and they kept it. Christians would never have sworn such an oath; they would have seen it as tempting God.

But I am wrong to speak of a Christian republic, because the two terms contradict each other. Christianity preaches only servitude and dependence. Its spirit favors tyranny so strongly that tyranny always benefits from it. True Christians are made to be slaves. They know it and hardly care, because this short life counts for too little in their eyes.

People will tell me Christian troops are excellent. I deny it. Show me one case. I know of no Christian troops. They will mention the Crusades. I do not dispute the Crusaders’ courage, but they were not Christians at all. They were the priests’ soldiers, citizens of the Church, fighting for their spiritual country, which the Church had somehow turned into a temporal one. Understood correctly, this is a return to paganism: because the Gospel sets up no national religion, Christians cannot wage a holy war.

Under the pagan emperors, Christian soldiers were brave. Every Christian writer says so, and I believe it: it was a case of honorable rivalry with the pagan troops. Once the emperors became Christian, that rivalry ended, and when the Cross had driven out the eagle, Roman valor disappeared completely.

But let us set political considerations aside, return to what is right, and fix our principles on this important point. We have seen that the right the social compact gives the Sovereign over the subjects does not go beyond the limits of public expediency.[5] So the subjects owe the Sovereign an account of their opinions only to the extent that those opinions matter to the community. Now it matters a great deal to the community that each citizen have a religion, because it will make him love his duty. But the dogmas of that religion concern the State and its members only insofar as they bear on morality and on the duties that the believer must do to others. Beyond that, each man may hold whatever opinions he likes, and the Sovereign has no business taking notice of them. The Sovereign has no authority in the other world, so whatever becomes of its subjects in the life to come is not its concern, as long as they are good citizens in this life.

There is therefore a purely civil profession of faith. The Sovereign should fix its articles, not exactly as religious dogmas, but as social sentiments, since without them no one can be a good citizen or a faithful subject.[6] The Sovereign cannot force anyone to believe them. It can, however, banish from the State anyone who does not, and it banishes him not for impiety but as an anti-social being, unable to love the laws and justice truly or to give up his life for duty when needed. If anyone, having publicly accepted these dogmas, acts as though he does not believe them, he should be put to death. He has committed the worst of all crimes: lying before the law.

The dogmas of civil religion ought to be few, simple and precisely worded, without explanation or commentary. These are its positive dogmas: the existence of a mighty, intelligent and beneficent Divinity, who has foresight and providence; the life to come; the happiness of the just; the punishment of the wicked; the sanctity of the social compact and the laws. Its negative dogmas I limit to one: intolerance, which belongs to the forms of worship we have rejected.

I think those who separate civil intolerance from theological intolerance are mistaken, because the two cannot be told apart. We cannot live at peace with people we believe to be damned; loving them would mean hating God, who punishes them. We simply have to either bring them back or torment them. Wherever theological intolerance is accepted, it is bound to have some civil effect,[7] and once it does, the Sovereign is no longer Sovereign, even in worldly matters. From then on the priests are the real masters, and kings are merely their ministers.

There is no longer, and cannot be, an exclusive national religion. So every religion that tolerates others should be tolerated, provided its dogmas contain nothing contrary to the duties of citizenship. But whoever dares to say _Outside the Church there is no salvation,_ should be driven out of the State, unless the State is the Church and the prince the pontiff. That dogma is good only under a theocratic government, and under any other it is fatal. The reason Henry IV is said to have given for joining the Roman religion should make every honest man leave it, and any prince who can reason even more so.

If the clergy has even a little sense, I will not say courage, it will take no notice and go its way. It will calmly allow the appeals, summonses, decrees and seizures, and in the end it will remain the master. It is not, I think, a great sacrifice to give up a part when one is sure of securing the whole.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 9 — Conclusion
paragraphs: I have now laid down the true principles of political right and tried to give the State a basis of its own. Next I should strengthen it through its dealings with other States: the law of nations, commerce, the right of war and conquest, public right, leagues, negotiations, treaties and so on. But all of this is a new subject, far too large for my narrow scope. I should have kept within narrower limits throughout.
